course.title: Mechanisms and Machine Design
course.description: How linkages, cams, gears, shafts, bearings, springs and bolts make machines move, last and fit together.
course.audience: Adults who have done Engineering: Structures and Machines and want to see how real machines are put together. They know forces, moments, stress, simple gear ratios and levers, and basic trigonometry.

paragraphs: A windscreen wiper turns the steady rotation of a motor into a sweep of 60 degrees, and a planetary gear set fits a fivefold reduction of speed inside the width of its own ring gear, with every shaft on one axis. Machines of this kind are built from a small number of parts, bars pinned into linkages, cams, gears, shafts, bearings, springs and bolts, and machine design is the study of how each of those parts moves and how much load it can carry, and for how long.

Most of the questions a designer asks about these parts can be settled with a short calculation done by hand. Counting the links and pins of a mechanism tells you how many motors it needs before anything has been drawn to size, the ratio of two tooth counts gives the speed ratio of a gear pair, and the cube of a ratio of loads tells you how much sooner an overloaded ball bearing will wear out. Calculations like these let you look at a machine and explain why it moves as it does, and find the part most likely to fail, including a part that carries its load easily once and still cracks after a million repeats.
outcomes: You'll be able to count a mechanism's freedoms and judge a four-bar linkage.
You'll be able to size a spur-gear pair and read a planetary train.
You'll be able to estimate bearing life, spring rates and bolt preload.
You'll be able to read a tolerance fit and judge a fatigue risk.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Engineering: Structures and Machines, Physics: Motion and Forces.

modules.title: Linkages and cams
modules.description: How a few rigid links and a profiled disc turn steady rotation into useful, controlled motion.

modules.title: Gears in depth
modules.description: Why gear teeth mesh smoothly, how epicyclic and worm trains reach big ratios, and what the teeth push on.

modules.title: Shafts, bearings and springs
modules.description: What carries the torque, what lets it spin, and what stores the energy.

modules.title: Joints, fits and failure
modules.description: Holding parts together, controlling how well they fit, and predicting how they break.

concepts.title: Links and joints
concepts.summary: A link is a rigid body; a joint is a connection that allows some relative motion and blocks the rest.

concepts.title: Mobility
concepts.summary: For a planar mechanism, M = 3(n - 1) - 2*j1 - j2, where n counts links including the fixed frame, j1 counts one-freedom joints and j2 counts two-freedom joints.

concepts.title: Grashof condition
concepts.summary: If the shortest plus the longest link is no more than the sum of the other two, at least one link can rotate fully.

concepts.title: Transmission angle
concepts.summary: The angle between the coupler and the output link; near 90 degrees the coupler pushes the output efficiently, and below about 40 degrees the linkage jams or wears.

concepts.title: Stroke
concepts.summary: In a slider-crank with no offset the slider travels twice the crank radius.

concepts.title: Quick return
concepts.summary: When the forward and return strokes take different crank angles, the ratio of the longer to the shorter is the time ratio, (180 + a)/(180 - a) for offset angle a.

concepts.title: Cam profile
concepts.summary: The cam's outline fixes the follower's displacement for every cam angle.

concepts.title: Motion law
concepts.summary: Constant velocity, simple harmonic and cycloidal motion trade peak speed and acceleration against smoothness.

concepts.title: Module
concepts.summary: Module m = pitch diameter / number of teeth in mm; two gears mesh only if their modules match.

concepts.title: Involute tooth
concepts.summary: An involute curve keeps the speed ratio constant even if the centre distance is slightly off, because contact stays on one fixed line of action.

concepts.title: Pressure angle
concepts.summary: The angle between the line of action and the common tangent of the pitch circles; 20 degrees is standard.

concepts.title: Epicyclic train
concepts.summary: A sun, planets on a carrier and a ring share an axis, so a large ratio fits in a small volume.

concepts.title: Worm drive
concepts.summary: A worm of N starts drives a wheel of Z teeth with ratio Z/N, and may lock if friction beats the lead angle.

concepts.title: Tooth force
concepts.summary: The tooth force is normal to the tooth; its tangential part carries the torque, its radial part pushes the gears apart.

concepts.title: Torsion
concepts.summary: A solid round shaft carrying torque T has surface shear stress 16T/(pi d^3) and twists by TL/(GJ).

concepts.title: L10 life
concepts.summary: The number of million revolutions that 90 percent of identical bearings survive: L10 = (C/P)^p.

concepts.title: Bearing types
concepts.summary: Plain bearings run on a lubricant film and suit high load at low speed; rolling bearings trade a small start-up friction for rolling contact.

concepts.title: Spring rate
concepts.summary: k = G d^4 /(8 D^3 N) for a helical compression spring with wire diameter d, mean coil diameter D and N active coils.

concepts.title: Wahl factor
concepts.summary: The shear stress in the wire is raised by a curvature factor Kw = (4C-1)/(4C-4) + 0.615/C, where C = D/d.

concepts.title: Preload
concepts.summary: A bolt works as a stiff spring pulling parts together; the initial tension is preload.

concepts.title: Joint constant
concepts.summary: C = kb/(kb+km) is the share of an added load that the bolt carries; the rest relieves clamping.

concepts.title: Fit
concepts.summary: The relationship between a shaft and a hole: clearance, transition or interference.

concepts.title: Basic-hole system
concepts.summary: The hole is fixed with zero lower deviation (H); fits vary by shaft deviation letters.

concepts.title: Fatigue
concepts.summary: Repeated stress far below yield can grow a crack until the part breaks.

concepts.title: Goodman line
concepts.summary: sa/Se + sm/Su = 1/n combines alternating and mean stress into a safety factor.

lessons.title: Counting what a mechanism can do

lead.text: The bar in the figure lies in a plane, and its position needs three numbers: how far it is along x, how far along y, and the angle it has turned through. Each of the three can change without either of the others changing, which is what makes them three *independent* movements, and each is called a **degree of freedom**.

A rigid piece of a mechanism is called a **link**, and whatever ties two links together is a **joint**: it lets some relative motion through and blocks the rest. The commonest is the **pin joint**, a pin through a hole in each link, which allows one link to turn about the other and blocks both sliding movements. The ground the machine stands on counts as a link as well, and is called the **frame**.

afterFigure.text: Switch to the second view and pin one end of the bar to the frame. That end can no longer slide in x or in y, so two of the three freedoms are gone, and what remains is the turn about the pin. A joint is therefore best understood through what it *takes away*, and a pin joint takes away two.

reveal.text: The pin removes two of the six freedoms and leaves four. The next screen counts the freedoms of a whole chain of bars in the same way.

lead.text: Take a mechanism of n links, one of which is the frame. The frame does not move, so only the other n − 1 links have freedoms to give, and if they were all free they would have 3(n − 1) between them. Every joint then takes some of those freedoms away: a pin joint takes two, since it fixes where the two links meet and so blocks both slides. A sliding joint, in which one link runs in a groove in another, also takes two, because it blocks the other slide and the turn.

Joints that remove two freedoms are counted together as j1. A joint that removes only one, such as the contact between a cam and its follower, where the surfaces may still slide and roll over one another, is counted as j2. The number of freedoms left is called the **mobility**, written M, and it is the number of inputs a mechanism needs before its motion is fully decided:
The planar count is usually called the Chebyshev–Grübler–Kutzbach criterion, after three engineers who each stated a version of it.

steps.headline: Count the mobility of a four-bar linkage: a crank, a coupler and a rocker pinned together and to the frame.

workedSteps.text: Count the links, and include the frame: the frame, the crank, the coupler and the rocker.
Count the joints. Each of the four corners is one pin joining two links, so there are four and all four are j1. There are no j2 joints.
Put n = 4 into the first term of the formula.
Each of the four pins takes away 2.
The difference is the mobility. One input, such as a motor on the crank, fixes the position of every other link.

reveal.text: The count gives 0, and it agrees with the picture: a triangle holds its shape however hard it is pushed, because each side fixes the distance between two corners.

lead.text: The figure applies the count to four arrangements. The triangle comes out at 0: it is a **structure**, which is exactly what the trusses of the earlier course were made of. The four-bar gives 1, and the five-bar gives 2, so a five-bar needs two motors before its coupler point goes where you want it.
The cam is the case that needs both kinds of joint. The pivot and the guide are j1 joints, and the contact between cam and follower is a j2 joint, so n = 3, j1 = 2 and j2 = 1.

afterFigure.text: A mobility of 1 means that **one input fully decides the motion**, and that is what a machine wants: turn the crank and everything else follows.

steps.headline: Find the mobility of a cam with a flat-faced follower that slides in a guide in the frame.

workedSteps.text: Count the links: the frame, the cam and the follower.
The cam turns on a pin in the frame, and the follower slides in a guide in the frame. Both remove two freedoms.
The cam touches the follower along a line, and surfaces in contact can still slide and roll. That joint removes one freedom.
The three counts go into the same formula as for the four-bar.

lead.text: It is easy to forget the frame, because it is drawn as hatching on the ground and not as a bar. The first view of the figure draws it as link 1, and the count gives M = 1. The second view leaves it out, so that n falls to 3 while the four pins are still there, and the formula gives −2, a mobility that has no meaning. Every answer found without the frame will be wrong by exactly 3, the freedoms of one link.
The formula counts joints and links but knows nothing about their lengths, so some arrangements with parallel links of equal length can move although the count says 0.

blocks.text: A sheet of card lying flat on a table can be pushed left and right, pushed towards and away from you, and turned about any point, and these three movements are all that is open to it while it stays on the table. Each independent movement is called a *degree of freedom*, and a body moving in a plane has three of them: two to say where it is, and one to say through what angle it has turned.

Push a drawing pin through one corner of the card into the table and two of the three are gone at once, since that corner can no longer go anywhere, which leaves only the turning. Every machine in this course is built of rigid pieces joined in this way, so a short piece of bookkeeping, three freedoms for every free piece and a deduction for each connection, tells you **how many motors a machine needs** before you have drawn anything more than its outline.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the links and joints of a planar linkage, work out its mobility, and say whether it is a structure or a mechanism.
intro.whyItMatters: A drawing of a mechanism tells you how many inputs it needs before any force or dimension is known.

recap.keyIdea: The mobility M = 3(n − 1) − 2×j1 − j2 counts the inputs a planar mechanism needs, and a value of 0 means a structure.

blocks.text: You counted three freedoms for each moving link and took away two for each pin or slide and one for a cam contact, remembering that the frame is a link. A four-bar gives 1, a five-bar gives 2 and a triangle gives 0, which is why trusses are rigid and why one crank can drive a slider-crank.
The count is blind to link lengths, so it describes the typical case and the geometry settles the special ones.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the four-bar, with its mobility of 1, and asks from its four lengths whether the crank can turn all the way round.

lessons.title: Four-bar linkages

lead.text: The loop in the figure is made of four links, and each has a name. The one fixed to the ground is the **frame**, 60 mm long. The link pinned to the frame and turned by a motor is the **crank**, 20 mm. The link on the other side of the frame, which only swings, is the **rocker**, 40 mm, and the link that joins the two moving ends, 50 mm, is the **coupler**.

Step the figure through four positions of the crank. The crank goes round without difficulty, but the rocker moves only within the dashed arc, 60 degrees wide, and the two ends of that arc are reached when the crank and coupler lie along one straight line, folded or stretched out.

afterFigure.text: A linkage in which one link turns fully and the opposite one rocks is called a **crank-rocker**.

reveal.text: The rocker covers its 60 degrees in one direction and then back, once for each turn of the crank, which is why the sweep is as steady as the motor.

lead.text: Not every set of four lengths gives a link that turns fully. Name the shortest length s, the longest l, and the other two p and q. If **s + l ≤ p + q**, the loop is called **Grashof**, and at least one link, the shortest, can make a full turn relative to the others. If s + l > p + q, no link can, whatever order the bars are in, and every link only rocks.

The reason is geometry. For a link to turn all the way round, the other three must be able to fold back along it at one moment and stretch out along it at the opposite moment. A long link on one side and a short one on the other leave no room for either, so the test finds the case in which the two longest sides are too long to let the shortest one pass.
The rule is credited to Franz Grashof, a German engineer of the nineteenth century.

steps.headline: Apply the test to the loop of 20, 50, 40 and 60 mm, then to a loop of 30, 40, 60 and 80 mm.

workedSteps.text: In the first set the shortest link is 20 mm and the longest is 60 mm.
The other two links are 50 and 40 mm.
Compare the two sums. 80 is less than 90, so the first loop is Grashof, and with the 20 mm link as the crank it is the crank-rocker that opened this lesson.
In the second set s = 30 and l = 80, and the others are 40 and 60, so p + q = 100.
The sum of the shortest and longest is larger than the sum of the others, so the loop is not Grashof and every link only rocks.

reveal.text: The sums are 90 and 100, so the loop is Grashof with 10 mm to spare. The next screen shows that one set of lengths can still make three different machines, depending on which link is the frame.

lead.text: Grashof's test says that a link can turn; it is the choice of frame that says which. The figure uses the same four lengths, 30, 40, 60 and 60 mm. When the shortest link, 30 mm, is the crank and sits next to the frame, the linkage is a **crank-rocker**. When it is the frame itself, both links pinned to the frame turn fully and the linkage is a **double-crank**. When it is the coupler, opposite the frame, the coupler turns fully while both links pinned to the frame only rock, and the linkage is a **double-rocker**.

Switch to the last view, in which the 30 mm link is joined with 40, 60 and 80 mm. Now 30 + 80 is greater than 40 + 60 and the linkage is not Grashof: it is a **triple-rocker**, in which no link goes all the way round.

reveal.text: The shortest link turns fully because it is the coupler, while both links pinned to the frame only rock. Moving the frame to the shortest link would instead make both of them turn fully.

lead.text: A linkage that can move may still be unable to carry a load. The coupler is a link pinned at both ends, and a link of that kind pushes or pulls only along its own length. At the rocker's pin that push meets the rocker at some angle, called the **transmission angle**, measured between coupler and rocker at their joint. Only the part of the push that is at right angles to the rocker turns it, and that part is the push multiplied by the sine of the transmission angle.

In the first view of the figure the angle is 51.3 degrees, so sin 51.3° = 0.78 of the push turns the rocker, and in the second view the angle is 125.1 degrees, which is 54.9 degrees from a straight line and gives a slightly larger useful fraction, sin 54.9° = 0.82. The last view is a different linkage, with a 30 mm frame, 50 mm coupler and rocker, and at its worst position the angle falls to 11.5 degrees, so only sin 11.5° = 0.20 of the push is useful and most of it squeezes the pin instead.

afterFigure.text: Designers commonly try to keep the angle above about 40 degrees at every position, a rule of thumb that also applies when the angle is above 90 degrees, since what matters is the distance from a straight line.

steps.headline: Find the transmission angle of the 20, 50, 40, 60 mm linkage with the crank at 90°, from the three sides of the triangle at the rocker pin.

workedSteps.text: With the crank standing at right angles to the frame, the crank pin is 20 mm above the frame's left pivot and the rocker pin is 60 mm along it, so the distance between them is the hypotenuse of a 60 by 20 right triangle.
The triangle at the rocker pin has sides 50 (coupler), 40 (rocker) and BD (the distance between the crank pin and the rocker pin). The law of cosines gives the angle opposite BD.
The top is 2500 + 1600 − 4000, which leaves only 100.
A calculator with its inverse cosine key set to degrees turns that cosine into an angle.

reveal.text: Each angle is judged by its distance from the nearest straight line, 0° or 180°. For the four positions those distances are 45°, 75°, 70° and 15°, and the smallest is the worst.

lessons.orientation: Say from four link lengths whether a four-bar can turn fully, name the type from where the frame is, and judge the transmission angle.
lessons.nextAction: Slider-cranks and quick returns: find the stroke of a slider-crank and the time ratio of a quick return.

blocks.text: Pin four bars of 20, 50, 40 and 60 mm into a loop and bolt the 60 mm bar to a table. Turn the 20 mm bar by hand and it goes all the way round, while the 40 mm bar opposite it swings to and fro through 60 degrees, and no further. That arrangement, a short crank turning a rocker, is the one behind a windscreen wiper, in which a motor at steady speed produces a steady sweep.

Replace the 50 mm bar by one of 30 mm and the loop is spoilt: no bar will now go all the way round. A test that fits on one line decides this before any metal is cut, and a second measure, the angle at which one bar pushes on the next, decides whether a loop that does move can also carry a load.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say from four link lengths whether a link can turn fully, name the linkage, and find where it transmits force badly.
intro.whyItMatters: A linkage that can turn is no use to a machine if its coupler cannot push the output round.

recap.keyIdea: If s + l ≤ p + q a four-bar has a link that can turn fully, and its transmission angle shows how well it carries a load.

blocks.text: Grashof's test compares the sum of the shortest and longest links with the sum of the other two, and the shortest link's place, as crank, frame or coupler, gives the crank-rocker, double-crank or double-rocker. The test says nothing about force, which is the job of the transmission angle: the push the coupler gives the rocker is multiplied by the sine of that angle, so an angle near zero or near 180 degrees means a jammed linkage.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson replaces the rocker by a slider, which turns a crank's rotation into a straight stroke and gives engines their reciprocating motion.

lessons.title: Slider-cranks and quick returns

lead.text: In a **slider-crank** the crank turns about a fixed centre, the **connecting rod** joins the crank pin to the slider, and the slider moves along a line through the crank centre.

Call the crank radius r and the rod length l, and measure the crank angle t from the line of the slider. The crank pin is r cos t along that line, and the rod, tilted at some angle, reaches the rest of the way: its horizontal part is √(l² − r² sin² t), because the crank pin stands r sin t to one side of the line and the rod must span that height. Adding them gives the slider position:

afterFigure.text: x = r cos t + √(l² − r² sin² t)
With r = 50 mm and l = 200 mm the three views give 250 mm at 0°, 193.6 mm at 90° and 150 mm at 180°.

reveal.text: At a right angle the rod is tilted but the crank term has vanished, so the slider sits just inside the rod's own length from the centre.
The stroke belongs to the crank alone, and the rod only moves the whole range along the line.

lead.text: The ends of the slider's travel are the two positions in which crank and rod lie in one line: stretched out, where x = l + r, and folded, where x = l − r. The difference is the **stroke**, 2r, and l has cancelled out. A longer rod therefore shifts the whole range outward without lengthening it. At each end the slider stops and reverses, so its speed there is zero, and the crank positions at which this happens are called the **dead centres**.

The rod does change *how* the slider gets from end to end. With a 200 mm rod the curve is close to a cosine and the slider is nearly halfway at 90°, but with a 100 mm rod the curve leans: at 90° the slider has already gone further than halfway (86.6 mm against the halfway mark of 100 mm), and the slider is slower on one half of the stroke than on the other.

diagram.alt: Two graphs of slider position against crank angle for a 50 mm crank. With a 200 mm rod the curve is nearly symmetrical about the halfway line; with a 100 mm rod it is lopsided. Both go over the same 100 mm range.
diagram.caption: The dashed line is halfway between the two ends. At 90 degrees the slider is below the halfway mark, and much more so with the short rod.

steps.headline: Find the slider position for r = 50 mm and l = 200 mm with the crank at 60°.

workedSteps.text: The crank pin contributes r cos t to the slider's position.
The height of the crank pin above the slider line is r sin t, and the rod must span it.
The rod's horizontal reach is the square root of l² less that height squared: 40000 − 1875.
The slider position is the crank's part plus the rod's part.

lead.text: A quick return changes the timing of the cycle while the crank still turns steadily. In the figure the slider line has been moved to 50 mm *above* the crank centre, an offset. The slider's two ends are still the stretched-out and folded positions, but now the crank lies along two different lines from the centre in those two positions, and those lines are not on a single straight line. The angle between them is called **α**; here, with r = 30 mm, l = 100 mm and an offset of 50 mm, it comes to 23.0 degrees.

Between the folded and the stretched-out positions the crank turns through 180° − α one way and 180° + α the other, so one stroke takes the crank through the larger angle. We call that one the forward stroke, and the other the return. A crank turning at a steady speed therefore spends more time on the forward stroke than on the return, in the ratio:

afterFigure.text: time ratio = (180° + α) ÷ (180° − α)

For α = 23.0° the ratio is 203.0 ÷ 157.0 = 1.29, so the forward stroke takes 29% longer than the return. A shaper uses the slow stroke for cutting, where it wants smooth speed, and the quick one to bring the tool back.

diagram.alt: A slider-crank whose slider line is 50 mm above the crank centre, with a 30 mm crank and a 100 mm rod. At the two ends of the stroke the crank lies on the two lines from the centre to the slider, and those lines make an angle of 23.0 degrees. The crank turns 203.0 degrees for one stroke and 157.0 degrees for the other.

steps.headline: A crank turns at 60 rpm, so a cycle takes 1 s. With α = 30°, find the time of each stroke and say what the offset has changed.

workedSteps.text: The forward stroke turns the crank through 180° + 30° = 210°. A full turn takes 1 s.
The return turns it through 180° − 30° = 150°.
The two stroke times must add up to the 1 s of the whole cycle.

reveal.text: The same equation works both ways. Larger α gives a larger ratio, but α can never reach 180° because the return would then take no time.

lessons.orientation: Find the stroke and slider position of a slider-crank, and the time ratio that an offset gives a quick return.
lessons.nextAction: Cams and followers: read a displacement diagram and find the follower's peak speed.

blocks.text: A crank of 50 mm radius turns about a fixed centre, and a 200 mm rod joins its end to a slider held in a straight groove, so that each turn of the crank pushes the slider 100 mm out and draws it 100 mm back. The slider's distance from the crank centre at any crank angle t is x = r cos t + √(l² − r² sin² t), which gives 250 mm when the crank is stretched out in line with the rod and 150 mm when it is folded back against it.

This arrangement, the **slider-crank**, is the piston and connecting rod of an engine, the plunger of a pump and the ram of a shaper, so the one formula sizes all of them. It also shows that the slider must stop and reverse at each end of its travel, which means that its speed cannot be steady even when the crank's is, and an offset version of the same arrangement lets a shaper cut on a slow stroke and return on a quick one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the stroke and position of a slider-crank and the time ratio of a quick return.
intro.whyItMatters: The slider-crank turns a motor's rotation into a straight push, so its formulas size every engine and pump.

recap.keyIdea: A slider-crank's stroke is twice the crank radius, and offsetting the slider line by an angle α makes the strokes take (180° + α) and (180° − α) of the crank's turn.

blocks.text: You found the slider's position from the crank angle, saw that the rod length drops out of the stroke and only reshapes the motion, and measured an offset's angle α from the two dead-centre lines. The time ratio (180° + α) ÷ (180° − α) is greater than 1 for any offset, and it shares the cycle without changing the work done.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson replaces the crank and rod by a cam, which can produce any motion a designer draws, not only the curve a crank gives.

lessons.title: Cams and followers

lead.text: A **cam** is a shaped disc that turns on a shaft and pushes on a **follower**, a link that is held in a guide and rides on its edge. Whatever motion the follower is to have can be drawn first as a **displacement diagram**: lift on the vertical axis, cam angle on the horizontal. The one in the figure has four parts. The follower **rises** 20 mm during the first 120 degrees, **dwells** at the top, staying still while the cam keeps turning, until 180 degrees, **returns** over the next 120 degrees, and dwells at the bottom for the last 60.

The outline of the cam is built from that diagram. The circle of smallest radius that the follower ever touches is the **base circle**, 30 mm here, and at each cam angle the cam's radius is the base-circle radius plus the lift, so at 120 degrees it is 30 + 20 = 50 mm.

afterFigure.text: The outline and the diagram must not be confused. The diagram plots lift against *angle*, and its shape would be the same for a cam of any base circle, whereas the outline is a closed curve whose size depends on the base circle and on the follower.

diagram.alt: A disc cam with a base circle of 30 mm and a follower resting on top, beside its displacement diagram. The diagram plots lift against cam angle: a rise of 20 mm over 120 degrees, a dwell to 180 degrees, a return over the next 120 degrees, and a dwell to 360.
diagram.caption: The dot on the graph shows the lift at the cam angle shown. The cam's outline and the graph are different curves. Use the buttons to turn the cam.

reveal.text: A 90° rise at 60 rpm lasts a quarter of a second, which sets the time T for the rise that the motion laws on the next screens use.

lead.text: The simplest motion law gives the follower the same speed throughout the rise, which draws a straight sloping line on the displacement diagram.

reveal.text: Constant velocity looks gentle in the middle of the rise, but at its two ends the follower must change speed in no time at all, which makes it the worst law at the corners.

lead.text: Lifting h in a time T gives an average speed of h ÷ T, which for 20 mm in 0.25 s is 80 mm/s, and each motion law is a different way of spending that time. **Constant velocity** runs at 80 mm/s throughout, and is the only law with the lowest peak speed, but its speed jumps from 0 to 80 at the start and back to 0 at the end, which needs a theoretically infinite acceleration and hammers the follower.

**Simple harmonic motion** follows s = (h/2)(1 − cos(πt/T)). It starts from rest smoothly in speed but is quickest in the middle of the rise: its peak speed is π/2 times the average, 125.7 mm/s, and its acceleration, whose peak is π²h/(2T²) = 1579 mm/s² (about 1.58 m/s²), is greatest exactly at the start and end, so there is still an abrupt jump of acceleration where the rise meets the dwell. **Cycloidal motion** has s = h(t/T − sin(2πt/T)/(2π)). Its peak speed is twice the average, 160 mm/s, and its peak acceleration 2πh/T² = 2011 mm/s² is larger, yet acceleration is zero at both ends, so the follower leaves and meets its dwells without a jolt.

afterFigure.text: The gentlest start is not the one with the most uniform speed: *smoothness is paid for with peak speed*.

diagram.alt: Three speed curves for a 20 mm rise in 0.25 s. Constant velocity holds 80 millimetres per second throughout and jumps from zero at each end. Simple harmonic motion peaks at 125.7. Cycloidal motion peaks at 160 and starts and ends smoothly.
diagram.caption: All three lift the follower 20 mm in 0.25 s, so all have the same average speed, 80 mm/s. Use the buttons to compare them.

steps.headline: Find the peak speed of a follower that rises 24 mm in 0.2 s with simple harmonic motion.

workedSteps.text: The average speed is the lift divided by the time of the rise.
For simple harmonic motion the peak speed is π/2 times the average, reached at mid-rise, where the cosine in the displacement is zero.
The average speed and this factor together fix the peak speed.

reveal.text: Cycloidal motion has the largest peak speed of the three, and the smallest abruptness at the ends of the rise.

lead.text: It is natural to think that a bigger lift needs a bigger cam, but the lift is the difference between the largest and smallest radius, and a cam of any size can have it. What the size does set is the **pressure angle**, the angle between the follower's direction of travel and the direction of the force the cam exerts on it, which is along the line at right angles to the cam surface. A large pressure angle means that a big part of the force is sideways, against the guide, instead of lifting the follower, and past a certain angle the follower sticks.

For a radial follower the tangent of the pressure angle is the slope of the lift diagram, the graph of lift against cam angle, measured in millimetres per radian, divided by the distance from the cam centre to the follower's tip: tan φ = (ds/dθ) ÷ (r_b + s). For a rise of 20 mm in 90 degrees with simple harmonic motion the slope at mid-rise is 20 mm per radian, and the lift is 10 mm there, so a 30 mm base circle gives tan φ = 20 ÷ 40, so φ = 26.6°, and a 60 mm base circle gives 20 ÷ 70, so φ = 15.9°.
Designers commonly aim to keep the pressure angle below about 30 degrees for a follower sliding in a guide, a rule of thumb rather than a limit.

reveal.text: The pressure angle falls as the base circle grows, which is the lever a designer has when a cam jams, apart from stretching the rise over a larger cam angle.

lessons.orientation: Read a displacement diagram, find a follower's peak speed under each motion law, and say why a small cam jams.
lessons.nextAction: Gear tooth geometry: find the pitch diameter and centre distance from a gear's module and tooth count.

blocks.text: An engine valve that has to rise 20 mm in a quarter of a second, stay open and close again is usually moved by a **cam**, a shaped disc on a turning shaft whose edge pushes on a follower. Every angle of the disc gives one lift of the follower, so a designer can draw the motion first, as a graph of lift against angle, and cut the outline to match it afterwards.

The rise can be drawn in several ways that look much alike on the page, yet at an average speed of 80 mm/s they make very different demands on the follower, since one of them calls for an infinite acceleration at the instant the rise begins and another for twice the average speed halfway up. Choosing between them, and choosing how large to make the disc, decides whether the follower runs smoothly or is struck a blow on every turn.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a displacement diagram, work out peak follower speed for the three motion laws, and see why base circle size matters.
intro.whyItMatters: A cam lets you draw the follower's motion first, and the choice of law decides how violently it is carried out.

recap.keyIdea: A cam turns a displacement diagram into a shaped outline, and the motion law trades peak speed against the smoothness of the start and finish.

blocks.text: The diagram of rise, dwell, return and dwell is not the cam's outline, which also depends on the base circle. Constant velocity has the lowest peak speed and an infinite acceleration at each corner, simple harmonic motion peaks at π/2 times the average, and cycloidal motion peaks at twice the average but begins and ends with zero acceleration.

recap.nextHook: The next module is about gears, which also transmit motion between shafts, and begins with why their teeth have the shape they do.

lessons.title: Why gear teeth are curved

lead.text: Each gear can be imagined as a smooth cylinder of the diameter at which the teeth would roll without slipping, and that diameter is called the **pitch diameter** d. The ratio of the gears is then the ratio of their pitch diameters, which equals the ratio of their tooth counts.

The size of the teeth is set by the **module** m, the pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth, in millimetres: m = d ÷ z, or d = m z. The figure uses m = 2 mm. A 20-tooth gear has a pitch diameter of 40 mm and a 45-tooth gear one of 90 mm, so the ratio is 2.25. The spacing between neighbouring teeth along the pitch circle is the circular pitch π m, which is 6.283 mm for m = 2.

afterFigure.text: Two gears can mesh only if their teeth are the same size, that is, if their modules are the same. Equal tooth counts do not suffice, and the pressure angle, the slant at which one tooth pushes on the other, has to match as well.

diagram.alt: Two spur-gear pairs drawn to scale with a module of 2 mm. A 20-tooth driver with a 45-tooth gear gives a ratio of 2.25, 444.4 revolutions a minute out and a centre distance of 65 mm. A 20-tooth driver with a 30-tooth gear gives a ratio of 1.5 and 666.7 revolutions a minute.
diagram.caption: The dashed circles are the pitch circles, which touch at one point on the line between the centres. Use the buttons to change the second gear.

reveal.text: A pitch diameter is the one dimension of a gear that cannot be measured directly with a caliper, because it lies half-way up the teeth, which is why the module is used to find it.

lead.text: In mesh the two pitch circles touch at a single point, on the line joining the centres. The distance between centres is therefore one pitch radius of each gear added together, a = (d₁ + d₂) ÷ 2, and since d = m z this becomes a = m(z₁ + z₂) ÷ 2. For a pair with a module of 2 and 65 teeth between the two gears it is 2 × 65 ÷ 2 = 65 mm.

The tooth tips stand one module above the pitch circle, so the outside diameter is d_a = m(z + 2), not m z. To find the module of an unknown gear you divide its outside diameter by z + 2, and the pitch diameter, which is not the outside diameter, cannot be read from the blank gear directly.

steps.headline: Find the pitch diameters, centre distance and ratio of a pair of module 2.5 mm gears with 16 and 40 teeth.

workedSteps.text: The pitch diameter is the module times the number of teeth.
The two gears have the same module, 2.5 mm, which is the condition for meshing.
The centre distance is half the sum of the pitch diameters.
The ratio is the ratio of tooth counts, or equally of pitch diameters.

reveal.text: The ratio depends on the base circle radii, and those do not change when the centres move, which is the geometry the next screen builds.

lead.text: Wind a string round a circle, called the **base circle**, hold the end taut and unwind it. The end of the string traces a curve called an **involute**. At every moment the string is straight and tangent to the base circle, and it meets the curve at a right angle, because the end is turning about the point where the string leaves the circle. The length of the straight string is also exactly the arc of the circle that has been unwrapped.

Gear teeth are cut as involutes of the base circle, and the reason follows from the second fact. When two such teeth touch, the contact force is at right angles to both surfaces, and that direction is a *fixed* straight line that is tangent to both base circles. Contact therefore always lies on that one line, and the ratio of the two turning speeds stays equal to the ratio of the base-circle radii at every instant. It also stays the same if the centres are moved apart a little, since neither base circle changes.

afterFigure.text: The involute's geometry makes the ratio exactly constant, which keeps the output smooth, and it tolerates small errors in centre distance, which is why gears of this kind are the standard.

diagram.alt: A string unwound from a circle, called the base circle, with its end tracing a curve, the involute. The string is straight and always at right angles to the curve, and its length equals the arc of the base circle that has been unwrapped.
diagram.caption: The curve drawn by the end of the string is an involute. Use the buttons to unwrap the string a little more each time.

reveal.text: The base circle of the 20-tooth gear is 37.59 mm across, and the involute starts there. The pitch circle lies above it, where the teeth do their work.

lead.text: The straight line tangent to both base circles passes through the pitch point, and it is called the **line of action**. Contact between the teeth lies on it at every moment, and the angle between it and the common tangent of the pitch circles, the dashed vertical line, is the **pressure angle** φ. The standard value is 20 degrees, and the base diameter is d cos φ.

Two practical limits follow. The **contact ratio** must be greater than 1, so that the next pair of teeth is touching before the last pair has parted. And a gear with too few teeth has its tooth bases cut away, which is called **undercut**; for a 20-degree pressure angle the theoretical limit is 2 ÷ sin²φ = 17.1, so a pinion needs about 17 teeth or more.

diagram.alt: A 20-tooth and a 45-tooth gear of module 2 mm drawn to scale. The line of action is tangent to both base circles, passes through the pitch point where the pitch circles touch, and makes the pressure angle of 20 degrees with the common tangent there.
diagram.caption: Contact between the teeth always lies on the green line. Its angle to the vertical dashed tangent at the pitch point is the pressure angle.

blocks.text: A pair of gears with 20 and 45 teeth turns one shaft 2.25 times for every turn of the other, and the ratio comes from nothing more than counting teeth. But two cylinders of 40 and 90 mm pressed together would also turn at that ratio, until the load made them slip, so the teeth have to do something that the ratio alone does not describe: they must carry the force without changing the ratio as they roll into and out of contact.

The shape that does it is an involute, drawn by a string unwound from a circle, and the size of the teeth is a single number called the module. Those two ideas decide whether any two gears can be put together, and how far apart their shafts must be.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find a gear's pitch diameter, module and centre distance, and say why an involute tooth keeps the speed ratio constant.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing gears from a catalogue comes down to matching module and pressure angle, and then to arithmetic on tooth counts.

recap.keyIdea: Gears mesh when module and pressure angle match, their centre distance is m(z₁ + z₂)/2, and involute teeth keep the ratio constant.

blocks.text: The pitch diameter is m z, the outside diameter is m(z + 2), and the centre distance is half the sum of the pitch diameters. The involute is what a string draws when unwound from the base circle, and all contact then lies on a fixed line of action, at 20 degrees to the common tangent for the standard gear.

lessons.title: Planetary and worm gears

lead.text: A single pair of gears is practical up to a ratio of about 6 or 10 to 1, because the larger gear has to be larger still. An **epicyclic** or **planetary** train fits a large ratio on a single axis. It has a **sun** gear at the centre, several **planet** gears that mesh with the sun and turn about their own axes while also circling it, a **carrier**, the arms on which the planets are mounted, and an outer **ring** gear with teeth on its inside that the planets also mesh with.

The sun, the carrier and the ring all turn about the same axis. Mobility counting gives the train two inputs, so to use it you *hold one part still, drive a second, and take the output from the third*. Which part you hold decides the ratio. The planets are not idle: they carry the motion from the sun to the ring, and it is the carrier on which they are mounted that usually delivers the output.

afterFigure.text: Their size does not appear in any ratio. It only sets the size of the ring, because the planets must span the gap between sun and ring: Z_ring = Z_sun + 2 Z_planet. With a sun of 20 teeth and a ring of 80, each planet has (80 − 20) ÷ 2 = 30 teeth.

reveal.text: With 33 teeth the planets here are larger than the sun, and nothing in the ratio depends on that choice.

lead.text: The most common arrangement holds the ring, drives the sun and takes the output from the carrier. With the ring held still, the planets that the sun drives must roll round inside the ring, and they carry the carrier with them, so the carrier turns more slowly than the sun does. The result is:
ratio = 1 + Z_ring ÷ Z_sun
For a sun of 20 teeth and a ring of 80 teeth the ratio is 1 + 80 ÷ 20 = 5, so a sun at 1000 rpm gives a carrier at 200 rpm.

afterFigure.text: The '1' in the formula is the carrier's own turn. The sun turns once relative to the carrier for each turn of the carrier itself, so the sun's turns per carrier turn are the ring-to-sun tooth ratio plus that one.

steps.headline: Find the output speed of a planetary set with a 16-tooth sun and an 80-tooth ring, with the ring fixed, when the sun turns at 1800 rpm.

workedSteps.text: The planets span the gap between the sun and the ring, so each planet has (80 − 16) ÷ 2 teeth.
The ratio, sun to carrier, is one plus the ring's teeth over the sun's.
The carrier is the output, and it turns slower than the sun by the ratio.

reveal.text: The formula only needs the two tooth counts of sun and ring, which is why a catalogue of ratios can be tabulated from them.
The carrier turns at 800 rpm, not at a fifth of the ring's speed, so which part is held matters more than the tooth counts do.

lead.text: Hold the sun, drive the ring and take the carrier. The planets now roll round the fixed sun, and the carrier follows them, but the ring that drives them is large and the carrier takes only a share of its speed. The ratio of ring speed to carrier speed is 1 + Z_sun ÷ Z_ring, so the carrier turns at 1 ÷ (1 + 20 ÷ 80) = 0.8 of the ring's speed. That is 800 rpm for a ring at 1000 rpm: a mild step-up in torque, not a large reduction.

Hold the carrier instead and the planets turn only on their own axes, as idlers. The sun drives them and they drive the ring *in the opposite direction*, with ratio −Z_ring ÷ Z_sun = −4 in the figure's third view. A planetary set can therefore give a large reduction, a small one or a reversal, from one set of gears, and automatic gearboxes use exactly that by braking different parts.

lead.text: A **worm** is a screw thread that meshes with a toothed **wheel** whose axis is at right angles to it. The number of separate threads running along the worm is its number of **starts**, N. One turn of the worm moves the wheel on by N teeth, so a wheel of Z teeth turns once for every Z ÷ N turns of the worm, and the ratio is Z ÷ N, to 1. A single-start worm with a 40-tooth wheel gives 40 to 1 in one stage.

How far the thread advances along the worm in one turn is its **lead**, which for a single-start worm equals the axial pitch, 5 mm in the example the figures use. If you unroll one turn of the thread flat it makes a right triangle with the lead as its height and the circumference π d as its base. The angle at the foot of that triangle is the **lead angle** l, so tan l = lead ÷ (π d).

reveal.text: More starts mean a lower ratio but a steeper thread, which matters for the question that the next screens take up: can the wheel turn the worm?

steps.headline: Find the lead angle of a worm with a 5 mm lead and 20 mm pitch diameter, and say whether it self-locks when the friction coefficient is 0.1.

workedSteps.text: Unroll one turn of the thread: the base of the triangle is the circumference π d.
The height of the triangle is the lead, 5 mm, so the tangent of the lead angle is the height over the base.
The lead angle is the angle with that tangent.
Friction holds a load on any slope up to the friction angle, which is the angle whose tangent is the friction coefficient.
The lead angle is now set against the friction angle.

lead.text: Friction between thread and tooth resists sliding as long as the push along the thread is shallow enough. For a coefficient of friction μ, sliding begins when the surface's slope exceeds the **friction angle**, arctan μ. Here μ = 0.1 gives 5.71°. The first view of the figure shows the thread with a lead angle of 4.55°, below that, so the wheel cannot turn the worm and the drive is **self-locking**: a hoist built this way holds its load when the motor stops.

It is not true that every worm locks. The second view uses a coarser thread of lead 20 mm: the lead angle is 17.7°, well above 5.71°, and the wheel *can* drive the worm. The same trade appears in the efficiency: the steeper thread wastes less in friction, which is why a self-locking worm is inefficient and a back-drivable one is not.

afterFigure.text: Treat self-locking as a likelihood and not as a brake. Friction varies with lubrication and wear, and vibration can let a locked drive creep, so a load that must not fall still needs a proper brake.

lessons.orientation: Find the ratio of a planetary train for each way of holding it, and the ratio and lead angle of a worm drive.
lessons.nextAction: Gear forces and shafts: resolve a tooth force and find the stress that a shaft carries.

blocks.text: A planetary gear set with a 20-tooth sun and an 80-tooth ring gives a reduction of 5 to 1 in a package no wider than its ring, with its input and output on one axis, and by holding a different one of its parts it can instead give a much milder change of speed or reverse the output altogether. A worm drive gives 40 to 1 in a single stage, and with a thread shallow enough it cannot be driven backwards from the output at all.

Neither arrangement can be worked out by counting the teeth on a pair of gears, since in a planetary set the planets turn about centres that are themselves moving, and in a worm drive the force acts along a screw thread.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out the ratio of a planetary train for each way of holding it, find a worm drive's ratio, and judge whether it self-locks.
intro.whyItMatters: Hubs, automatic gearboxes, hoists and steering all rely on these two arrangements.

recap.keyIdea: A planetary train's ratio depends on which part is held, and a worm self-locks only when its lead angle is below the friction angle.

blocks.text: Ring fixed and sun driven gives 1 + Z_ring ÷ Z_sun, sun fixed and ring driven gives a ratio of 1 + Z_sun ÷ Z_ring, and holding the carrier reverses the output. A worm gives a ratio of Z ÷ N, and tan l = lead ÷ (π d) decides whether l falls below the friction angle.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the forces that all these gears carry, resolves a tooth force into its components, and follows the torque into the shaft.

lessons.title: What gears push on, and what shafts carry

lead.text: Where two teeth touch, the force between them is at right angles to both surfaces, so it lies along the [[line of action|The fixed line, tangent to both base circles, on which the teeth touch. Met in 'Why gear teeth are curved'.]], 20 degrees from the tangent to the pitch circle. It helps to split it along two directions. The **tangential force** Ft acts along that tangent, at the pitch radius r, and it is the part that makes the torque, so Ft = T ÷ r. The **radial force** Fr acts along the line from one centre to the other, so it pushes the gears apart, and since the two make a right angle with the normal force at the pressure angle φ, Fr = Ft tan φ and the normal force is Ft ÷ cos φ.

For a torque of 40 N·m on a gear of 50 mm pitch radius, the first view gives Ft = 40 ÷ 0.05 = 800 N, Fr = 800 × tan 20° = 291.2 N, and a normal force of 851.3 N. The mistake to avoid is to treat the torque as the force: torque is a moment in newton-metres, and the force it makes at the teeth depends on the radius.

afterFigure.text: The tangential force bends the shaft sideways as well as twisting it, and the radial force adds a second bending load at right angles to the first, so the bearings of a gear shaft carry both of them. The second view shows that the same 800 N turns a bigger gear with a larger lever arm, which is how a torque of 40 N·m on the small gear becomes 90 N·m on the large one.

reveal.text: The tooth force is large: a small radius makes a large force from a modest torque, which is why small pinions need strong teeth.

steps.headline: Resolve a tangential tooth force of 600 N for a 20° pressure angle into its radial and normal parts.

workedSteps.text: The pressure angle is the angle between the normal force and the tangent. In the force triangle, the tangential force is the side next to that angle.
The radial force is the side opposite the angle, so it is the tangential force times the tangent of the angle.
The normal force is the hypotenuse, which is the tangential force over the cosine.
The two components act in different directions, and only one of them lies along the line between the gear centres.

reveal.text: The stress falls by a factor of 8, not 2 or 4, and the next screens show why the diameter is cubed.

lead.text: The torque in a shaft is rarely given. What is given is the power P in watts and the speed n in revolutions per minute. The speed in radians per second is ω = 2π n ÷ 60, and power is torque times angular speed, so T = P ÷ ω. For the example of 5 kW at 1500 rpm, ω = 2π × 1500 ÷ 60 = 157.08 rad/s and T = 5000 ÷ 157.08 = 31.83 N·m.
The relation shows that torque and speed trade off for the same power. A shaft that turns half as fast carries twice the torque.

reveal.text: The torque is 23.9 N·m, a little under the 31.83 N·m of the 5 kW example, because power and speed both changed.

lead.text: A shaft under a torque T is twisted, and each cross-section turns a little relative to the next. The shear in the material is zero on the axis and grows in a straight line to the surface, as the arrows in the figure show, and the largest stress is at the outside. For a solid round shaft of diameter d it is τ_max = 16 T ÷ (π d³).

For the 31.83 N·m of the earlier example and d = 20 mm, τ = 16 × 31.83 ÷ (π × 0.02³) = 20.3 MPa. The cube answers the earlier prediction: the same torque on a 40 mm shaft gives 2.5 MPa, one eighth as much. The shaft also twists, by the angle θ = T L ÷ (G J), where L is its length, G the shear modulus of the material and J = π d⁴ ÷ 32 the polar second moment of area, which grows with the *fourth* power of the diameter.

afterFigure.text: At a keyway or a shoulder the real stress is higher than this formula says, by a stress concentration factor. A first estimate that ignores these should be treated as a lower bound.

blocks.text: A gear of 50 mm pitch radius carrying a torque of 40 N·m pushes on the teeth of its partner with a force of 800 N along the tangent, because a torque is a force multiplied by the radius at which it acts. Gear teeth push along a line tilted 20 degrees from that tangent, though, so the same contact also forces the two gears apart, and that second push goes into the shafts and their bearings as well.
Behind the gear, the shaft carries the torque by twisting, and the twist sets up a shear stress in the metal.

intro.whyItMatters: A shaft that is too thin twists or breaks, and a gear's tooth force is what first loads it.

recap.keyIdea: The tooth force splits into Ft = T ÷ r and Fr = Ft tan φ, and a solid shaft's shear stress 16T ÷ (π d³) falls with the cube of the diameter.

blocks.text: Torque is not a force. The tangential force is the torque divided by the pitch radius, the radial force is smaller by tan φ and loads the bearings, and the shaft's torque follows from power and speed as P ÷ ω. Shear stress in a solid round shaft is greatest at the surface, and doubling the diameter cuts it to one eighth.

lessons.title: Bearings and how long they last

lead.text: Every rotating shaft needs a bearing, and a bearing is judged by its friction and its life. In a **plain bearing** the shaft turns inside a bush with a thin film of oil between them. Once the shaft is up to speed it drags oil into the gap, and the film carries the load so that the metal surfaces do not touch. A plain bearing takes high loads at low speed well, tolerates shock, is quiet and is cheap, but at start-up, before the film forms, the surfaces touch and friction is high.

A **rolling bearing** puts hard elements between two rings, an inner race fixed to the shaft and an outer race fixed to the housing, with a cage keeping the elements apart. **Balls** touch the races at a point and give the least friction, **rollers** touch along a line and carry more load for the same size. Rolling replaces much of the sliding, so start-up friction is small, although the contact stresses in the tiny areas of contact are very large, which is what limits their life.

reveal.text: A plain bearing earns its low wear in long steady runs, once the oil film has formed, and loses it while the film is missing, as it is at every start.
Life falls to an eighth, not a half, which is the law that the next screen states.

lead.text: The maker of a bearing states its **dynamic load rating** C: the load, in kilonewtons, that gives a life of one million revolutions. At a lighter load P the life is longer, and the relation, found from fatigue tests, is **L10 = (C ÷ P)^p** million revolutions, with p = 3 for ball bearings and p = 10/3 for roller bearings. For C = 14 kN and P = 2 kN the life of a ball bearing is (14 ÷ 2)³ = 343 million revolutions.

The 10 in L10 is the percentage that fail: 343 million is the life that 90% of a large batch of identical bearings reach or exceed. It is not the life of each bearing, since 10% fail earlier, and the typical bearing, the median one, lasts about five times as long. Because of the cube, the load matters a great deal: the figure shows that raising the load from 2 kN to 4 kN reduces the life from 343 to 42.9 million revolutions, an eighth.

steps.headline: Find L10 for a bearing with C = 16 kN carrying P = 2 kN, first as a ball bearing and then as a roller bearing.

workedSteps.text: The ratio of the rating to the load is what is raised to the power.
A ball bearing uses the exponent 3, so the ratio is cubed.
A roller bearing uses the exponent 10/3 in place of 3, which is slightly higher.
For the same C and P, a roller bearing therefore outlasts a ball bearing.

lead.text: Revolutions are not a useful unit for a machine that runs a stated number of hours a day. If the bearing turns at n revolutions per minute it makes 60 n revolutions an hour, so the life in hours is L10h = L10 × 10⁶ ÷ (60 n). For 343 million revolutions at 1500 rpm that is 343 × 10⁶ ÷ 90 000 = 3811 hours.

The same bearing at twice the speed lasts half as many hours, since the revolutions run out sooner. A designer works backwards from the hours the machine must run to the L10 required, and from that to the rating C of the bearing to choose.

reveal.text: About 2083 hours is nearly three months of running, so a bearing under a steady load in a continuous machine is often chosen for a much larger C.
The ratio of rating to load is 6 instead of 5, and life is 216 million revolutions instead of 125: a modest change in C ÷ P gives a large change in life.

blocks.text: A ball bearing rated at 14 kN that carries a load of 2 kN is expected to last 343 million revolutions, which at 1500 rpm is 3811 hours of running. Its balls touch their tracks over areas so small that a modest rise in load raises the stress there sharply, and since that stress is repeated on every revolution, the life of a bearing depends on its load far more strongly than you might expect.

Even the figure of 343 million revolutions is less definite than it looks, because it is the life that nine bearings out of ten reach, called the **L10 life**, while one in ten fails sooner. Knowing how that life is defined and how it changes with load and speed lets you choose a bearing for the hours a machine has to run, and judge when a plain bearing, which has no balls or rollers at all, would serve better.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate the L10 life of a ball or roller bearing, convert it to hours, and say when a plain bearing is the better choice.
intro.whyItMatters: Bearings are among the most often replaced parts of a machine, and a life estimate says when.

recap.keyIdea: L10 = (C ÷ P)^p million revolutions, with p = 3 for balls and 10/3 for rollers, and 90% of bearings reach it.

blocks.text: Life depends on the load through a power, so doubling the load on a ball bearing cuts its life to an eighth, and a roller bearing of the same rating outlasts a ball bearing. Hours follow from revolutions by dividing by 60 n, and a plain bearing, which rides on an oil film, can still be the better choice for shock and noise.

lessons.title: Springs

lead.text: A spring is a part that deflects under load and returns when the load is removed, and in a machine it is mostly used to store energy or to apply a steady force. A **linear spring** has a force proportional to its compression x, F = k x, where k is the **spring rate** in newtons per millimetre.

The energy stored is the work done in compressing it, and since the force rises from zero to k x the average force is half of the final one: **E = ½ k x²**. The shaded triangle is that work, 195.3 N·mm at 10 mm. Compress it twice as far, to 20 mm, and the force doubles but the energy is *four* times as large, 781.2 N·mm.

reveal.text: Energy grows with the square of the compression, which is why a spring can store a large amount of energy for a small increase in deflection.
The rate falls to an eighth: the wider coil makes the wire twist much more for the same load, which the next screen explains.

lead.text: The load acts along the spring's axis, but the wire runs round the coil at a distance D ÷ 2 from that axis, so at every section the load tries to *twist* the wire, as a torque of F D ÷ 2 about its own length. A coil spring is a torsion bar wrapped into a helix. The wire is not stretched, and the failure is a shear failure.
Adding up the twist of all the active turns gives the rate of the spring:

afterFigure.text: k = G d⁴ ÷ (8 D³ N)

Here G is the shear modulus of the wire, d the wire diameter, D the mean coil diameter and N the number of **active coils**, those free to deflect. The wire diameter appears to the fourth power in the numerator, so thicker wire makes a much stiffer spring, while the coil diameter appears as D³ in the denominator: a wider coil is *softer*. For d = 2 mm, D = 16 mm, N = 10 and G = 80 000 N/mm², k = 3.906 N/mm.

steps.headline: Find the rate of a spring with d = 2.5 mm, D = 20 mm, N = 8 and G = 80 GPa, which is 80 000 N/mm².

workedSteps.text: Work out the powers: the wire diameter to the fourth, and the coil diameter cubed.
The top of the fraction is G d⁴. The bottom is 8 D³ N.
The rate is the top of the fraction divided by the bottom.

lead.text: Springs are often combined. When they are placed **in parallel**, side by side between the same two plates, they deflect by the same amount, and their forces add, so their rates add: k = k₁ + k₂. Two springs of 6 and 3 N/mm give 9 N/mm. When they are placed **in series**, end to end, the same force passes through each, and the deflections add, which means that the *flexibilities* 1 ÷ k add:

afterFigure.text: The same springs in series give 1 ÷ k = 1 ÷ 6 + 1 ÷ 3 = 1 ÷ 2, so k = 2 N/mm, softer than either. The error to avoid is adding the stiffnesses of springs in series, which gives 9 and is the rule for the other arrangement.

lead.text: The torsion formula for the wire gives a basic shear stress τ = 8 F D ÷ (π d³). For F = 40 N, D = 16 mm and d = 2 mm that is 8 × 40 × 16 ÷ (π × 8) = 203.7 MPa. The wire is bent into a coil, though, and this raises the stress on the inner side of each turn, where the wire's surface is shorter. The correction is the **Wahl factor** K_w, which depends on the spring index C = D ÷ d:
With C = 16 ÷ 2 = 8, K_w = 31 ÷ 28 + 0.615 ÷ 8 = 1.184, so the stress that matters is 1.184 × 203.7 = 241.2 MPa. Tight coils, with a small index, raise the factor: a spring of index 4 has K_w = 1.40.

steps.headline: Find the corrected shear stress in the wire of a spring with D = 15 mm and d = 2.5 mm under F = 50 N.

workedSteps.text: The spring index is the coil diameter over the wire diameter.
The index goes into the Wahl factor.
The torsion formula gives the basic stress in the wire, before any correction for the coil.
The stress the wire has to withstand is the basic stress times the Wahl factor.

lead.text: A mass m on a spring of rate k, pulled aside and released, oscillates at its **natural frequency**, f = (1 ÷ 2π) √(k ÷ m), where k is in N/m and m in kg. For a mass of 0.5 kg on the 3.906 N/mm spring, k = 3906 N/m, √(3906 ÷ 0.5) = 88.4 rad/s and f = 14.1 Hz. A stiffer spring or a lighter mass raises the frequency, and because of the square root a fourfold change in k or m changes it only by a factor of two.

The frequency matters because a load that pushes at about the natural frequency makes the oscillation grow, which is called resonance. A spring has frequencies of its own, too, in which its coils move along the wire as a wave. In a fast machine, such as a valve spring, a loading at one of those frequencies produces **surge**, in which the coils bounce against each other and the stress is above the calculated value.

reveal.text: The mass is heavier and the spring softer than the 14.1 Hz case, so the frequency falls to 8 Hz, which is the direction that the formula says.

blocks.text: A coil spring wound from 2 mm steel wire, 16 mm across the coil and with 10 active turns, takes about 39 N to compress by 10 mm, and at a load of 40 N the wire inside it carries a shear stress of about 241 MPa. Both numbers follow from the spring's dimensions and the stiffness of its steel, through formulas short enough to work by hand.
The same formulas tell you how much energy a spring stores, how two springs behave when they are set end to end or side by side, and how fast a mass resting on one will bounce.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the rate of a helical spring, combine springs, correct its stress for curvature, and find the natural frequency of a mass on it.
intro.whyItMatters: Springs set the force and the timing of valves, latches, seats and suspensions.

recap.keyIdea: A helical spring's rate is k = G d⁴ ÷ (8 D³ N), combined by adding stiffnesses in parallel and flexibilities in series, and its natural frequency is (1 ÷ 2π)√(k ÷ m).

blocks.text: The load twists the wire, so the rate depends on d⁴ and falls with D³, and the Wahl factor raises the stress for the curvature. Series and parallel follow different rules, and the natural frequency of a mass on a spring rises with stiffness and falls with mass, through a square root.

lessons.title: Bolted joints and preload

lead.text: Tightening the nut stretches the bolt a small amount, like a very stiff spring, and the bolt pulls back, pressing the plates together. That tension is the **preload**, and the force it puts on the plates is the clamp force, which is equal to it.

It is tempting to see a bolt as a rigid pin that holds two parts together, but the right model is a pair of springs: the bolt, which is stretched, and the clamped parts, which are squeezed by the same force. The stiffnesses of these two springs decide what happens when the joint is loaded.

diagram.alt: A side view of a bolted joint with two plates clamped between a bolt head and a nut. Tightening stretches the bolt and squeezes the plates. When a sideways load acts on the plates, friction between them, from the clamp force, carries it, and the bolt is not loaded in shear.
diagram.caption: The green dashed line is the friction surface between the plates. Use the buttons to apply a sideways load.

reveal.text: The preload fixes both the clamp force and the starting tension in the bolt, and it is the number that a tightening procedure aims for.

lead.text: How tight should a bolt be? A greater preload gives a greater clamp force and so more friction, but the preload cannot exceed what the bolt can take without a permanent stretch, the **proof load**, which is the proof strength times the **stress area** of the thread. A common target is about 75% of the proof load, which leaves a margin. For an M10 bolt of class 8.8, with a stress area of 58 mm² and a proof strength of 580 MPa, the proof load is 580 × 58 = 33.6 kN and 75% of it is 25.2 kN.

Class 8.8 means a nominal tensile strength of 800 MPa and a yield of 640 MPa, from the 8 and the .8. A preload is set by the torque on the nut: T = K F d, in which F is the preload, d the nominal bolt diameter and K a **nut factor**, about 0.2 for ordinary dry steel bolts. For the 25.2 kN preload of the M10 bolt above, T = 0.2 × 25 200 × 0.01 = 50.4 N·m. The torque is a poor measure of the preload, since most of it is lost in friction in the threads and under the nut, and K varies from joint to joint.

afterFigure.text: A bolt tightened past its proof load stretches permanently and then no longer clamps.

reveal.text: The target preload is a fraction of the proof load, not of the tensile strength, which would be much higher.

steps.headline: Find the tightening torque for a preload of 20 kN on a 10 mm bolt with a nut factor of 0.2.

workedSteps.text: Convert to SI units: the preload in newtons and the diameter in metres.
The torque is the nut factor times the preload times the diameter, T = K F d.
The torque is proportional to the preload, so the 25.2 kN preload found earlier needs 25.2 ÷ 20 = 1.26 times this torque on the same bolt.

reveal.text: Only a fraction goes to the bolt, which the next screen works out by treating both parts as springs.

lead.text: Pull on the joint with an external load P. The bolt stretches a little more, and the plates, which were being squeezed, relax by the same small distance. Because the two have different stiffnesses, they change their forces by different amounts. The bolt, with stiffness kb, rises by C P and the clamped parts, with stiffness km, lose (1 − C) P, where C is the **joint constant**:
C = kb ÷ (kb + km)

The diagram plots force against deformation, with the flexible bolt on the right and the stiffer parts on the left. With kb : km = 1 : 4 the constant is 0.2, so an external load of 10 kN raises the bolt tension from 20 to 22 kN and lowers the clamp force from 20 to 12 kN.

afterFigure.text: The bolt carries a small share because it is the *more flexible* part, and the clamped parts, being stiff, give up their squeeze. This is a good thing for fatigue, since the bolt's load changes by only a fifth of the external load.

diagram.alt: A joint diagram with force upward and deformation sideways. The bolt's line is shallow because the bolt is flexible, and the clamped parts' line is four times steeper. With a preload of 20 kilonewtons and an external load of 10, the bolt tension rises to 22 and the clamp force falls to 12. At an external load of 25 the clamp force is zero.

lead.text: The clamp force is Fi − (1 − C) P, and it reaches zero when P = Fi ÷ (1 − C). For a preload of 20 kN and C = 0.2, that is 20 ÷ 0.8 = 25 kN. Beyond that point the plates open, the bolt takes the whole of the external load and the friction that held the joint is lost.

The margin to separation is a reason for a high preload: a greater Fi moves the separation load up. It is limited by the proof load, so the design choice is to preload as high as is safe, then check that the external load stays well under the separation load.

The bolt takes only the share C of what is added.

blocks.text: An M10 steel bolt of class 8.8 can be tightened until it carries a tension of about 25 kN before it comes near the load that would stretch it permanently, and a spanner turned to a few tens of newton-metres is enough to put that tension in it. The stretched bolt presses the plates of the joint together, and the friction between the plates is what stops them sliding sideways, so a well-tightened bolt is not loaded in shear at all.

When an outside load then tries to pull the joint apart, the bolt and the clamped plates act as two springs in one load path, one stretched and one squeezed. How the load divides between them decides how much extra tension the bolt must carry and at what load the plates open, and so whether the joint keeps its grip.

lessons.title: Fits and tolerances

reveal.text: The band is 13 µm wide, and any size in it is acceptable: a tolerance is a permission, not an error.

lead.text: A machine tool cannot cut to the exact size on a drawing, and an exact size could not be measured anyway. A drawing therefore gives a **tolerance**, the band of sizes in which the part is acceptable. It is a *permission to vary*, not a record of an error, and any part inside the band is a good one. Tighter tolerances cost more, since they need slower cutting, better machines and more inspection, so the wide tolerances that the function allows are the best ones.

The standard system, ISO 286, describes the band with a letter and a number. The number is the tolerance grade, written IT: a higher number is a wider band, and the width also grows with the size of the part. For a nominal size of 25 mm, IT6 is 13 µm and IT7 is 21 µm. The letter gives the position of the band against nominal size: a capital letter is for a hole and a small letter for a shaft. A hole of 25 H7 runs from 0 to +21 µm, so its sizes are from 25.000 to 25.021 mm.

reveal.text: Every H hole starts at its nominal size, which is what makes H the basis of the system: the hole is made first, and the shaft is fitted to it.

lead.text: A **fit** is the relationship in size between a shaft and the hole it goes into. In the **basic-hole system** every hole is H, so its lower limit is exactly the nominal size, and the fit is chosen by moving the shaft's band with a letter. The reason is practical: holes are cut with fixed tools such as drills and reamers, while a shaft is turned to any size.

The figure shows three shafts for a 25 H7 hole. A **g6** shaft has deviations of −20 to −7 µm, so it is always smaller than the hole: that is a **clearance fit**. A **p6** shaft has deviations of +22 to +35 µm and is always larger: an **interference fit**, which has to be pressed in. A **k6** shaft, +2 to +15 µm, overlaps the hole's band, and whether there is a small gap or a small squeeze depends on the parts: a **transition fit**.

lead.text: When parts are stacked end to end, the tolerance of the whole stack depends on the tolerances of its parts. The **worst-case** method assumes that every part is at its extreme in the same direction at once, and simply adds them: three parts of ±0.10 mm give ±0.30 mm. This is safe, but it is pessimistic, since parts made independently seldom all stray the same way together.

The **statistical** method, root sum of squares, uses that fact. Independent variations combine as the square root of the sum of their squares, so three parts of ±0.10 give √(3 × 0.10²) = 0.173 mm, and the result grows with the *square root* of the number of parts, not with the number. A designer often uses the worst case where a fault is dangerous and the statistical method where a rare excess is tolerable.

blocks.text: A drawing of a shaft and the hole it runs in may carry the label 25 H7/g6, and those few characters fix the size of both parts without asking either to be exactly 25 mm. The hole may be bored to any size in a narrow band that starts at 25 mm and runs upwards, and the shaft turned to any size in a band that lies wholly below 25 mm, so every shaft made to the drawing will slide into every hole made to it, with a gap whose largest and smallest values are known in advance.

lessons.title: How parts fail

lead.text: A part can fail in three static ways: it **yields**, so that it is permanently deformed, it **fractures**, or it **buckles**. But a part can also break at a stress far below the yield strength if the stress is *repeated*. A crack starts at a tiny flaw or at a notch, grows a little with every cycle, and finally the part is left too thin to carry the load and breaks suddenly. This is called **fatigue**.

The usual record of it is an **S-N curve**: tests at different stress amplitudes S, plotted against the number of cycles N to failure, on log axes. In the figure the curve falls from 450 MPa at 10³ cycles to a knee at 10⁶ cycles and 200 MPa, and then runs flat. The flat level is the **endurance limit** Se: below it, a steel part is expected to last indefinitely. At 300 MPa the part in the figure fails after about 32 000 cycles. The idea was drawn from nineteenth-century tests of railway axles by August Wöhler.

afterFigure.text: Some materials, such as aluminium, have no such knee, and their curve keeps falling, so for them a life must be stated at a chosen number of cycles. A part that has survived many cycles has not been shown to be safe for ever, since the crack may be growing all the while.

diagram.alt: An S-N curve for a steel part on log axes: stress amplitude against cycles to failure. The line falls from 450 megapascals at a thousand cycles to a knee at 200 megapascals and a million cycles, then runs flat. At 300 megapascals the part fails after about 32 thousand cycles; at 180 it does not fail.
