reveal.text: About half of Su is the rule of thumb for steel, and the endurance limit of an actual part is lower, for reasons that the next screen gives.

lead.text: The estimate of half the tensile strength applies to a small polished test bar. A real part is rougher and larger, and surface scratches or machining marks start cracks, so the endurance limit is reduced by modifying factors for **surface finish**, **size** and **type of loading**.

A notch, a hole, a shoulder or a keyway forces the stress to flow around it and raises the local stress. The factor is the **stress concentration factor** Kt, which *multiplies* the nominal stress: the peak stress is σ_max = Kt × σ_nom. A hole in a plate has Kt of about 3, so a nominal stress of 30 MPa becomes 90 MPa at the edge of the hole. The stress concentration is why failures so often start at a hole or a corner, and it is added by multiplication, never by addition.

reveal.text: The peak is three times the average, and a crack will start where that peak is, not where the average is.

lead.text: Real parts rarely cycle about zero. A preloaded bolt or a valve spring never returns to zero stress, so it carries a steady **mean stress** sm, and each cycle swings about it by an **alternating stress** sa. A mean stress that is tensile makes the alternating part more damaging. The **Goodman line** joins the endurance limit Se on the alternating-stress axis to the tensile strength Su on the mean-stress axis, and a state of stress under that line is safe for infinite life. A factor of safety n is found from
sa ÷ Se + sm ÷ Su = 1 ÷ n

afterFigure.text: A part with Se = 200 MPa and Su = 500 MPa that is loaded with sa = 100 MPa and sm = 100 MPa gives 100 ÷ 200 + 100 ÷ 500 = 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7, so n = 1 ÷ 0.7 = 1.43. The two terms are the shares of the fatigue budget used by the alternating and the mean stress, and the sum must stay below 1.

steps.headline: Find the safety factor for Se = 200 MPa, Su = 500 MPa, sa = 80 MPa and sm = 100 MPa.

workedSteps.text: The alternating stress uses a share of the endurance limit.
The mean stress uses a share of the tensile strength.
The two shares add up to 1 ÷ n.

reveal.text: A safety factor of nearly 2 means that both stresses could rise by almost double before the part reached the Goodman line.

lead.text: A machine seldom runs at one stress. Miner's rule, a way of adding up the damage from different loadings, treats the life as a budget of 1. If a part is cycled n times at a stress whose life is N, it uses up the fraction n ÷ N of its life, and when the fractions from all the stresses add to 1, it is predicted to fail: **D = Σ nᵢ ÷ Nᵢ**.

A part that sees 10⁵ cycles at a stress whose life is 5 × 10⁵ uses 0.2, and 3 × 10⁵ cycles at a stress whose life is 10⁶ uses another 0.3, so D = 0.5 and half of the life is left. The rule is a rough guide, since the order of the loads matters, but it is simple.

steps.headline: Find the damage done by two blocks of cycles: 10⁵ cycles at a stress with life 4 × 10⁵, and 2 × 10⁵ cycles at a stress with life 10⁶.

workedSteps.text: The first block is 10⁵ cycles at a stress whose life is 4 × 10⁵.
The second block uses a fifth of the life.
Miner's rule adds the two fractions to give the total damage, and the part is predicted to fail when the total reaches 1.
A part that has survived those cycles has not been made immune.

lead.text: When a fatigued shaft is broken apart, the surface tells the story. The crack starts at a point, usually at the surface and often at a notch, and grows slowly, leaving smooth curved lines called **beach marks**, each a pause in the growth. When the remaining area can no longer carry the load, it breaks at once, in a rough **fast-fracture zone**.

The size of that final zone shows the stress. In the first view the crack has crossed most of the section before the break, so the stress was low. In the second the shaft broke after a small crack, so the stress was high. A failure investigator can therefore read both the position of the stress concentration and the loading from the broken part.

diagram.alt: A fatigue fracture surface of a round shaft. A crack starts at a point on the surface, grows slowly across the section, leaving curved beach marks, and the remaining area breaks suddenly in the final fast-fracture zone. A small final zone means a low stress; a large one means a high stress.
diagram.caption: The blue region is slow crack growth and the orange region is the final break. Use the buttons to compare a lightly loaded shaft with a heavily loaded one.

reveal.text: The part can be run for 220 000 more cycles at this stress by Miner's rule, which is a budget and not a guarantee, so a margin is kept.

lessons.orientation: Apply the Goodman line and Miner's rule, and judge where and why a part might fail by fatigue.
lessons.nextAction: Judge a mechanism from its freedoms and linkages to its gears, bearings, joints and fatigue life.

blocks.text: A steel part with a tensile strength of 500 MPa can carry a stress of 450 MPa for about a thousand cycles, yet it cannot carry 300 MPa for a hundred thousand, and at 180 MPa it can run indefinitely. The stress that finally breaks it is far below the stress it could carry once, because each repetition grows a crack too small to see, so how long the part lasts depends on how large the repeated stress is and how often it is applied.
Cracks of this kind almost always begin where the stress is locally higher than the average, at a hole, a shoulder or a keyway, and the final break comes suddenly.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read an S-N curve, apply Goodman's line to find a safety factor, and add up fatigue damage with Miner's rule.
intro.whyItMatters: Most failures of machine parts in service are fatigue failures, and they give no warning.

recap.keyIdea: A repeated stress below yield can grow a crack until the part breaks, and the Goodman line and Miner's rule turn that risk into a safety factor and a damage sum.

blocks.text: Notches multiply the nominal stress by Kt, and finish and size lower the endurance limit. The Goodman line, sa ÷ Se + sm ÷ Su = 1 ÷ n, gives a safety factor for a steady cycle, and Miner's rule adds the fractions n ÷ N used at each stress until the sum reaches 1.

questions.prompt: A bar in a plane has three freedoms. It is pinned to the frame at one end by a pin joint, which removes two of them. How many freedoms does it have now?
hints: Start from 3 and take away what the pin removes.
The pin stops the end sliding in x and sliding in y, so 3 − 2 is what remains.
That remaining freedom is the turn about the pin.
questions.onCorrect: The one freedom left is the turn about the pin, which is why a single bar on a pin can only swing like a pendulum.

misconceptions.feedback: Three is the free bar. The pin removes two of the three.
The pin removes two freedoms, not one.

questions.prompt: Why does the formula use n − 1 in 3(n − 1) rather than n?
hints: Ask what a link contributes before any pins are added.
The frame is the body that all other motion is measured against.

acceptedIdeas: The frame does not move, so it adds no freedoms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The frame does not move, so it adds no freedoms

questions.onCorrect: Motion is always measured against the frame, so the frame is counted in n but brings no freedoms of its own.

misconceptions.feedback: The frame has none: it is the reference that the other links move against.
Any link can be the input, and the input is chosen after the count, not before it.

choices.label: The frame does not move, so it adds no freedoms
One link must always be the input link, and it is left out
The frame has only one freedom, so it is counted separately

questions.prompt: Three bars are pinned together at their ends in a triangle, and one of them is the frame. With n = 3 and j1 = 3, what is the mobility?
hints: Subtract.
questions.onCorrect: A mobility of 0 means the pins leave no freedom at all, which is why a truss built of triangles is rigid.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the freedom of one free bar, before anything is pinned.
Check the arithmetic: 3(3 − 1) is 6, and the pins remove 6.

questions.prompt: With n = 3, j1 = 2 and j2 = 1, what is the mobility M of the cam and follower?
hints: The pivot and the guide are the full-strength joints, and the contact is the lighter one.
Two moving links bring 6 freedoms, then take away 4 for the two j1 joints.
Take away what the contact removes, and see what is left.
questions.onCorrect: One input, the turning of the cam, decides where the follower is, which is exactly what a cam is for.

misconceptions.feedback: A contact joint still takes away a freedom. Subtract it as j2.
The cam contact is a j2 joint, which removes a single freedom, not two.

questions.prompt: A slider-crank has a crank, a connecting rod, a slider and the frame, joined by 3 pin joints and 1 sliding joint. What is its mobility?
hints: The frame is one of the links, and both kinds of joint count as j1.
Add the pins to the slide to get j1.
Three moving links bring 9 freedoms; the j1 joints remove eight.
questions.onCorrect: A sliding joint removes two freedoms like a pin does, which is why the slider-crank has the same count as a four-bar.

misconceptions.feedback: The sliding joint is a j1 joint like the pins, so there are four of them.
Check the number of j1 joints: three pins and a slider make four.

questions.prompt: A planar linkage has 6 links including the frame and 7 pin joints. What is its mobility?
hints: Every pin is a j1 joint, and the frame is one of the six links.
Five moving links bring 15 freedoms.
The seven pins remove 14 of them.
questions.onCorrect: A mobility of 1 means one motor drives the whole six-link chain, as in the six-bar linkages used in some hoods and hinges.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the pins: seven of them remove 14 freedoms, not 13.
Subtract 14 from 15 again; the pins do not remove everything.

questions.prompt: An assembly of 5 links, one of them the frame, is joined by 6 pins, and its mobility is 3(5 − 1) − 2×6 = 0. What kind of assembly is it?
hints: What does a mobility of 0 leave free?
Nothing can move relative to the frame.
questions.onCorrect: Zero mobility is rigidity, so such an assembly can carry loads, which is the job of a structure.

misconceptions.feedback: A mobility of 1 would be a mechanism with one input; this count gives 0.
Two inputs would need a mobility of 2.
It can be built: it is simply rigid.

choices.label: A mechanism that cannot be built
A mechanism with two inputs
A structure
A mechanism with one input

questions.prompt: A mechanism has 5 links including the frame, 4 pin joints and 1 sliding joint. How many inputs does it need?
hints: Both kinds of joint count as j1.
Add the pins to the slide to get j1.
Four moving links bring 12 freedoms; the j1 joints remove ten.
questions.onCorrect: Two inputs are needed because 12 freedoms are offered and 10 are taken away.

misconceptions.feedback: Count 5 j1 joints, not 4: the sliding joint also removes two freedoms.
The sliding joint removes two freedoms, like a pin.

questions.prompt: In the loop of 20, 50, 40 and 60 mm the crank is turned once through a full circle at a steady rate. What does the rocker do during that one turn?
hints: Picture the rocker while the crank goes once round: it moves only within its 60-degree arc.
The ends of the rocker's range come where crank and coupler lie in one straight line.

acceptedIdeas: It swings out through its 60-degree arc and back once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It swings out through its 60-degree arc and back once

questions.onCorrect: One round trip per turn of the crank means a steadily turning motor gives a steady sweep, as in a wiper.

misconceptions.feedback: The rocker moves only within its 60-degree arc, so it never goes all the way round. Only the short crank can.
The mobility is 1, so each crank position fixes one rocker position, and the rocker cannot stay at one end while the crank keeps turning.
The rocker reaches an end of its arc when crank and coupler lie in one straight line, stretched out or folded. Count how often each of those happens in one turn.

choices.label: It swings to one end of its arc and stays there
It swings out through its 60-degree arc and back once
It turns once through a full circle, as the crank does
It swings out and back twice, once for each half-turn

questions.prompt: Four links are 30, 40, 60 and 60 mm. By how many millimetres does p + q exceed s + l, where s and l are the shortest and longest?
hints: Find s and l first, then p and q are the two that remain.
s + l is 90.
Subtract that from p + q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: s + l = 30 + 60 = 90 and p + q = 40 + 60 = 100, so the margin is 100 − 90 = 10 mm.

questions.onCorrect: A positive margin means the loop is Grashof: some link can turn fully. A negative one means no link can.

misconceptions.feedback: That is s + l. Work out p + q and take the difference.
Subtract the other way: p + q is the bigger sum here.

questions.prompt: In a Grashof four-bar the shortest link is fixed as the frame. The linkage is a double-___ (crank or rocker).
hints: With the shortest link as the frame, both links hinged to it can turn all the way round.
questions.onCorrect: With the shortest link fixed, both links pinned to it can turn fully, which is a double-crank: the drag-link linkage.

misconceptions.feedback: A rocker only swings. With the shortest link as the frame, both links pinned to it turn fully.

questions.prompt: In the 20, 50, 40, 60 mm linkage with the crank at 90°, cos μ = 0.025. What is the transmission angle μ, in degrees, to 1 decimal place?
hints: Use the inverse cosine key, marked cos⁻¹ or arccos, with the calculator set to degrees.
The cosine is close to 0, so the angle is close to 90°.
questions.onCorrect: At nearly 90° almost all of the coupler's push, sin 88.6° = 0.9997, turns the rocker, so this is close to the best position the linkage has.

misconceptions.feedback: That is cos μ. The transmission angle is the angle with that cosine.
That is 90° minus the answer. Take the inverse cosine of 0.025 directly.

questions.prompt: With the crank at 180° the same linkage has μ = 125.1° between coupler and rocker. Because it is above 90°, take its distance from a straight line: 180° minus that. What is that angle, in degrees?
hints: The angle is more than a right angle, so it leans past 90°.
Its distance from a straight line is what is left of a straight angle.
A straight angle is 180°, so subtract 125.1° from it.
questions.onCorrect: Poor transmission is judged by the angle's distance from a straight line, so 125° is as healthy as 55°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the angle itself. Judge it by its distance from a straight line.
That is 90° less the angle. Subtract from 180° instead.

questions.prompt: A loop has links of 25, 55, 45 and 70 mm. Is it Grashof?
hints: Pick out the shortest and longest first.
Compare their sum with the sum of the other two.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, some link can turn fully
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, some link can turn fully

questions.onCorrect: With 95 ≤ 100 a link can turn fully. Which one it is, and whether it is the crank, depends on where the frame goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the shortest plus the longest, 25 + 70, with the other two added, 55 + 45. The test pairs the shortest with the longest, not the two smallest.
The test uses only the four lengths. The frame decides which kind of linkage it is, not whether a link can turn fully.

choices.label: Yes, some link can turn fully
No, no link can turn fully
It cannot be said without the frame

questions.prompt: A Grashof four-bar has its shortest link as the crank, next to the frame. What kind of linkage is it?
hints: The shortest link turns fully. Ask what the link on the other side of the frame does.
questions.onCorrect: The shortest link is the crank when it is next to the frame, and the link across the coupler from it rocks.

misconceptions.feedback: A double-crank has the shortest link as the frame. Here the shortest link is the crank, and the link across from the frame only swings.
A double-rocker has the shortest link as the coupler, opposite the frame. Here it is next to the frame.
A triple-rocker is not Grashof, so no link turns fully. This linkage is Grashof, and its shortest link turns.

choices.label: Crank-rocker
Double-crank
Double-rocker
Triple-rocker

questions.prompt: A linkage has a 20 mm crank, 50 mm coupler, 50 mm rocker and 30 mm frame. With the crank at 0° the crank pin is 10 mm from the rocker pin. Find the transmission angle in degrees from cos μ = (50² + 50² − 10²) ÷ (2 × 50 × 50).
hints: Work out the top of the fraction first.
The top is 4900 and the bottom is 5000.
Take the inverse cosine.
questions.onCorrect: At 11.5° only sin μ, about 20%, of the coupler's force turns the rocker, so a load would jam this position.

misconceptions.feedback: That is cos μ. Find the angle whose cosine it is.
That is 90° less the answer. Take the inverse cosine of the fraction itself.

questions.prompt: In the loop of 30, 40, 60 and 80 mm, what is s + l, the shortest plus the longest, in millimetres?
hints: Pick out the shortest and the longest link.
They are the 30 mm and 80 mm links.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: Because 110 is more than the 100 of the other two, the shortest link cannot pass the others.

misconceptions.feedback: That is p + q, the sum of the other two links.
That is 30 + 40. Use the longest link, 80 mm.

questions.prompt: A slider-crank has crank radius 40 mm and a rod 160 mm long. Using x = r cos t + √(l² − r² sin² t), how far is the slider from the crank centre when the crank is at 90°, in millimetres, to 1 decimal place?
hints: At 90° the crank is square to the slider line, so the term with cos is zero and sin is 1.
Work out l² and r² separately.
Take the square root of their difference, 25600 less 1600.
questions.onCorrect: At 90° the slider is a little short of the rod length from the centre, because the rod is tilted between crank pin and slider.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rod length. The tilt of the rod makes the slider sit a little closer.
That is l − r. At 90° the distance is √(l² − r²).

questions.prompt: A crank of 20 mm radius gives a slider a stroke of 40 mm. The connecting rod is replaced by one 20 mm longer. What happens to the stroke?
hints: Think about where the slider is when crank and rod lie in one straight line, at each end of its travel.
questions.onCorrect: A longer rod moves both ends of the stroke outward by the same amount, so the distance between them stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer rod pushes both ends of the travel out by the same 20 mm, so the distance between them does not change.
The ends of the travel sit at l + r and l − r, and the rod length cancels when one is taken from the other.
Both ends of the travel move outwards together, so the gap between them neither grows nor shrinks.

choices.label: It becomes shorter
It stays the same
It grows a little
It grows by about 20 mm

questions.prompt: The crank is at 60° (r = 50 mm, l = 200 mm). The term r cos t is 25 mm, and under the root l² − r² sin² t = 40000 − 1875. What is x in millimetres, to 1 decimal place?
hints: First take the square root of 38125.
The root is about 195.3 mm.
Add the 25 mm from the crank term.
questions.onCorrect: The crank term and the rod term add: a part from the crank's reach and a larger part from the rod, tilted at this angle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the rod's part. Add the crank's part, r cos t.
The crank term is r cos 60° = 25 mm, not 50 mm.

questions.prompt: A quick-return mechanism makes the return stroke faster than the cutting stroke. What does it change about each cycle?
hints: Ask which quantities in a cycle the offset angle can change.

acceptedIdeas: How a cycle's time is split between the strokes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How a cycle's time is split between the strokes

questions.onCorrect: The crank still turns at one speed. The return stroke is faster because the crank turns through fewer degrees for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The force and the stroke are set by the machine, and the offset does not alter them.
The stroke is set by the crank and slider geometry, so the offset leaves its length alone.

choices.label: How much work the machine does in a whole cycle
How far the slider travels in each of its strokes
How a cycle's time is split between the strokes

questions.prompt: An offset slider-crank has α = 20°. The forward stroke takes 180° + α of crank turn and the return takes 180° − α. What is the ratio of forward time to return time, to 2 decimal places?
hints: Add α to a half turn, and subtract it from a half turn.
The two angles are 200° and 160°.
Divide the larger by the smaller.
questions.onCorrect: A ratio of 1.25 gives the cutting stroke 25% longer than the return, at the same crank speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. Put the longer stroke on top.
Divide 200 by 160, not 180 + 20 by 180.

questions.prompt: At 60 rpm one cycle takes 1 s. With α = 30°, the forward stroke takes 210/360 of that, 0.583 s. How long does the return stroke take, in seconds, to 3 decimal places?
hints: The return takes the remainder of the cycle.
It takes (180 − α)/360 of a second.
That is 150 divided by 360.
questions.onCorrect: The two stroke times add up to the one second of a cycle, whatever α is.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the forward stroke. The return turns through the smaller angle.
That would be α = 0. The return is shorter than half a cycle here.

questions.prompt: A shaper needs the cutting stroke to take 1.5 times as long as the return. Solve (180 + α) ÷ (180 − α) = 1.5 for α, in degrees.
hints: Multiply both sides by 180 − α.
That gives 180 + α = 270 − 1.5α.
Collect the α terms: 2.5α equals the difference of the constants.
questions.onCorrect: Quick returns of this kind are limited because α cannot approach 180°, which is why practical ratios stay under about 3.

misconceptions.feedback: Check: α = 30° gives 1.4, not 1.5.
That is 270 − 180. Divide by 2.5 to finish.

questions.prompt: A slider-crank has crank radius 35 mm and a rod 140 mm long. What is the stroke in millimetres?
hints: The stroke depends on the crank only.
It is twice one of the two lengths.
Double the crank radius.
questions.onCorrect: The rod length drops out because it adds to both ends of the stroke equally.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rod length, which does not set the stroke.
The slider travels the crank's diameter, which is twice this.

questions.prompt: With r = 50 mm and l = 200 mm and the crank at 90°, how far is the slider from the crank centre, in millimetres, to 1 decimal place?
hints: At 90° the cos term vanishes.
You need √(l² − r²).
40000 − 2500 is the number under the root.
questions.onCorrect: The slider is 6.4 mm short of the rod length here, and the shorter the rod the larger that shortfall.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the tilt of the rod.
That is l − r, the position at the inner end of the stroke.

questions.prompt: A quick-return offset gives α = 30°. What is the ratio of the forward-stroke time to the return-stroke time, to 1 decimal place?
hints: The forward stroke uses 180° + α of crank turn.
The two crank turns are 210° and 150°.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: A ratio of 1.4 means 58% of each cycle is spent cutting and 42% returning.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down: the longer stroke goes on top.
Divide 210 by 150, not 210 by 180.

questions.prompt: A cam turns at 60 rpm, so one turn takes 1 s. How long does a 90° rise take, in seconds?
hints: First find what fraction of a full turn 90° is.
One turn takes 1 s.
Multiply the fraction by the time for a turn.
questions.onCorrect: At a steady cam speed, time is proportional to cam angle, so the displacement diagram can be read as a graph against time too.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 180°. A 90° rise is a quarter turn.
That is the angle. Convert it to a fraction of a turn and then to time.

questions.prompt: Which motion law has a theoretically infinite acceleration at the start of the rise?
hints: Look for a law whose speed goes from zero to its full value at once.
questions.onCorrect: A jump in speed over no time needs infinite acceleration, which in practice is a hammer blow on the follower.

misconceptions.feedback: Its acceleration is finite, if abrupt, at the start.
Cycloidal is the law that begins with zero acceleration.
One of the three has an instant jump from rest to full speed.

choices.label: None of them
Cycloidal
Constant velocity
Simple harmonic

questions.prompt: A follower rises 24 mm in 0.2 s with simple harmonic motion. The average speed is 120 mm/s and the peak is π/2 times that. What is the peak speed in mm/s, to 1 decimal place?
hints: The peak is a fixed multiple of the average.
π/2 is about 1.571.
Multiply 120 by that.
questions.onCorrect: A smooth start costs a higher peak: simple harmonic motion tops the average by 57%, so the follower must go faster mid-rise.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average speed. The peak is π/2 times larger.
That is the cycloidal peak, twice the average.

questions.prompt: A follower rises 30 mm in 0.3 s with cycloidal motion, whose peak speed is twice the average. What is the peak speed in mm/s?
hints: Find the average speed first: lift divided by time.
The average is 100 mm/s.
Double it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Average = 30 ÷ 0.3 = 100 mm/s, so the peak is 2 × 100 = 200 mm/s.

questions.onCorrect: Cycloidal motion pays for its soft start and finish with the highest peak speed of the three laws, twice the average.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average speed. The cycloidal peak is twice that.
That is the simple harmonic peak, π/2 times the average.

questions.prompt: A radial follower is driven by a cam with a base circle of 40 mm. At mid-rise the slope ds/dθ is 20 mm per radian and the lift is 10 mm, so tan φ = 20 ÷ (40 + 10). What is the pressure angle φ in degrees, to 1 decimal place?
hints: Work out the fraction first: the slope over the distance from the cam centre.
The distance is 50 mm, so the fraction is 0.4.
Take the inverse tangent.
questions.onCorrect: A larger base circle gives a smaller pressure angle, which is why a cam that is small for its lift tends to jam.

misconceptions.feedback: That is tan φ. Find the angle with that tangent.
That is the 30 mm base circle's value. Here the distance is 40 + 10.

questions.prompt: A follower rises 30 mm in 0.3 s with simple harmonic motion. The average speed is 100 mm/s. What is the peak speed in mm/s, to 1 decimal place?
hints: Peak speed is a multiple of the average.
The multiple is π/2.
Multiply 100 by about 1.571.
questions.onCorrect: Simple harmonic motion's peak is π/2 times the average, whatever the lift and time are.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average speed. The peak is π/2 times larger.
That is the cycloidal peak, twice the average.

questions.prompt: Which law has zero acceleration at both the start and the end of the rise?
hints: Think about which law starts and ends most gently.
questions.onCorrect: Cycloidal motion has zero acceleration at both ends, so the follower leaves and meets its dwells without a jolt.

misconceptions.feedback: Its acceleration is infinite at the ends, not zero.
Its acceleration is greatest at the ends of the rise.

choices.label: Constant velocity
Cycloidal
Simple harmonic

questions.prompt: A cycloidal rise of 40 mm takes 0.5 s. What is the peak speed in mm/s?
hints: The average speed is lift ÷ time.
The average is 80 mm/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ω in rad/s. Divide by 2π.
That is k ÷ m. Take the square root and divide by 2π.

questions.prompt: What do we call the tension that a bolt carries after it is tightened, before any external load acts?
hints: It is a load that is put in 'beforehand'.
questions.onCorrect: The preload is the clamp force too: the bolt stretches by the amount the plates are squeezed, and the two forces are equal.

misconceptions.feedback: The proof load is the most the bolt can take without a permanent set. The tension put in by tightening is called something else.
The clamp force is what the bolt does to the plates, and it is equal to this tension. What is the tension in the bolt itself called?

questions.prompt: A bolt has a stress area of 58 mm² and a proof strength of 600 MPa. A preload of 75% of the proof load is wanted. What is the preload in kN, to 1 decimal place?
hints: The proof load is the proof strength times the stress area.
Take 75% of that, then convert to kN.
questions.onCorrect: Preload is set below proof strength so that the bolt is not stretched permanently and keeps its spring action.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole proof load. A preload of 75% of it is lower.
That is in newtons. Convert to kilonewtons.

questions.prompt: The tightening torque is T = K F d. Take K = 0.2, a preload F = 20 000 N and a bolt diameter d = 0.01 m. What is T in N·m?
hints: Multiply the three numbers together.
Then multiply by 0.01.
questions.onCorrect: Most of the torque goes into friction in the threads and under the head, which is why K matters so much.

misconceptions.feedback: That omits the diameter. Multiply by d in metres.
Check the units: F in newtons, d in metres.

questions.prompt: A bolt is tightened to 20 kN, and the plates it clamps are four times as stiff as the bolt. An outside load of 10 kN then tries to pull the joint apart. Roughly how much does the bolt's tension rise?
hints: The bolt stretches and the plates relax by the same small distance.
questions.onCorrect: The bolt takes a small share because the clamped parts are much stiffer, so they give up their squeeze before the bolt stretches.

misconceptions.feedback: The plates were already squeezed, and most of the outside load is taken by relieving that squeeze rather than by stretching the bolt further.
The load is not shared equally: the plates relax by the same small distance as the bolt stretches, and being stiffer they give up more force for it.
The bolt does stretch a little as the plates relax, so its tension rises, if only by a small part of the load.

choices.label: By the full 10 kN
By about 5 kN
Not at all, until the plates separate
By about 2 kN

questions.prompt: A joint has a joint constant C = 0.3, and an external load of 12 kN acts on it. How much does the bolt tension rise, in kN, to 1 decimal place?
hints: The added bolt load is C times the external load.
C is the bolt's share, as a decimal.
Multiply 0.3 by 12.
questions.onCorrect: The remaining 70% of the load relieves the clamping instead, so the plates squeeze less.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the clamp force lost, (1 − C) P. The bolt gets C P.
The bolt takes only a share of the external load.

questions.prompt: Why does the bolt carry only a small share of the external load?
hints: Compare the two stiffnesses in the joint constant.

acceptedIdeas: The clamped parts are much stiffer, so they give up their squeeze
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The clamped parts are much stiffer, so they give up their squeeze

questions.onCorrect: The joint constant kb ÷ (kb + km) is small when km is large, so most of the load goes to relieving the clamp.

misconceptions.feedback: It is the other way round. The bolt is the more flexible part.
Preload is set below proof strength, and the share is set by stiffness.

choices.label: The clamped parts are much stiffer, so they give up their squeeze
The bolt is tightened to its proof strength, so it cannot carry more
The bolt is much stiffer, so it moves less than the clamped parts

questions.prompt: A joint has a preload of 15 kN and a joint constant of 0.25. At what external load does the clamp force fall to zero, in kN? Use P = Fi ÷ (1 − C).
hints: Work out 1 − C first.
Divide the preload by it.
questions.onCorrect: The joint separates at a load larger than the preload, since the bolt itself takes a share of what is added.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the preload alone. The bolt also takes a share, so separation needs more.
That multiplies by 0.75. Divide by it.

questions.prompt: An M10 class 8.8 bolt has a preload of 18 kN in a joint with a joint constant of 0.25. An external load of 12 kN is applied. What is the total tension in the bolt, in kN?
hints: The bolt keeps its preload and adds C P.
Add the preload.
questions.onCorrect: The bolt sees preload plus a small share of the load, which is much less than the load alone, and fatigue life benefits from that.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the full external load. The bolt takes only the share C P.
That is the added part alone. Add the preload.
That is the clamp force, 18 − 0.75 × 12. The bolt's tension rises, by C P.

questions.prompt: Preload 25 kN, K = 0.2, bolt diameter 12 mm. What tightening torque is needed, in N·m?
hints: Use T = K F d with SI units.
questions.onCorrect: A wrench set to the torque gives the preload only as well as K is known, and K may vary by a quarter or more.

misconceptions.feedback: That omits the diameter. Multiply by d in metres.
That uses d in millimetres. Use metres.

questions.prompt: A joint has a joint constant of 0.25 and an external load of 8 kN. How much extra load does the bolt carry, in kN?
hints: The bolt's share is C times the external load.
C is the fraction the bolt takes.
Multiply 0.25 by the external load.
questions.onCorrect: The other 6 kN comes off the clamp force rather than going into the bolt.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the clamp force lost, (1 − C) P.
The bolt takes only a share of the external load.

questions.prompt: A bolt has a preload of 20 kN and the joint constant is 0.2. What external load separates the joint, in kN?
hints: Use P = Fi ÷ (1 − C).
Divide the preload by that.
questions.onCorrect: At 25 kN the clamp force is gone, and the bolt alone carries everything.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the preload alone. Divide by 1 − C to find separation.
That multiplies by 0.8. Divide by it.

questions.prompt: A shaft is allowed to be anywhere between 24.980 mm and 24.993 mm. What is its tolerance, the width of the permitted band, in mm?
hints: Subtract the lower limit from the upper.
The difference is a few thousandths of a millimetre.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 24.993 − 24.980 = 0.013 mm, which is 13 µm, the IT6 grade at this size.

questions.onCorrect: A tolerance is permission to vary: any shaft inside the band is a good one, and none needs to be exactly 25 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the upper limit. The tolerance is the width of the band.
That halves the band. The tolerance is the full width.

questions.prompt: A 40 mm hole of grade H7 has limits 0 and +25 µm from nominal. What is its largest permitted size in mm?
hints: Add the upper deviation to the nominal size.
25 µm is 0.025 mm.
40.000 plus that.
questions.onCorrect: H means the lower deviation is zero, so the hole's smallest size is exactly nominal.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deviation alone. Add it to the nominal size.
That subtracts the deviation. For H the hole grows upward from nominal.

questions.prompt: For 25 H7/g6 the hole is 25.000 to 25.021 mm and the shaft 24.980 to 24.993 mm. What is the minimum clearance, the smallest gap, in mm?
hints: The smallest gap comes from the smallest hole and the largest shaft.
The smallest hole is 25.000 mm.
Subtract the largest shaft, 24.993, from it.
questions.onCorrect: The minimum clearance is the g deviation itself, 7 µm, which is the margin that keeps the shaft from ever binding.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest gap, from the largest hole and the smallest shaft.
Use the hole's smallest size and the shaft's largest.

questions.prompt: A fit in which the shaft is always larger than the hole is called an ___ fit.
hints: The shaft has to be forced in, so the parts overlap.
questions.onCorrect: In an interference fit the parts must be pressed or heated into place, and they then grip by elastic stress.

misconceptions.feedback: A clearance fit has a gap at every size. Here the shaft is larger than the hole.
In a transition fit the result can be either a gap or a squeeze, depending on the parts chosen.

questions.prompt: For 25 H7/p6 the hole is 25.000 to 25.021 mm and the shaft 25.022 to 25.035 mm. What is the smallest interference in mm?
hints: The smallest squeeze comes from the smallest shaft and the largest hole.
The smallest shaft is 25.022 mm.
Subtract the largest hole.
questions.onCorrect: The smallest interference is only 1 µm, which still keeps the shaft larger than the hole.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest interference, from the largest shaft and the smallest hole.
That is the shaft's deviation. Subtract the largest hole size.

questions.prompt: Six parts each have a tolerance of ±0.05 mm. Using the root of the sum of squares, what is the statistical stack-up tolerance, in ± mm, to 2 decimal places?
hints: Square each tolerance and add the six squares.
0.05² = 0.0025, and six of them make 0.015.
Take the square root.
questions.onCorrect: Six parts give 0.12 against a worst case of 0.30: statistical stacking grows with √n, not n.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the worst case, the straight sum.
That is the four-part stack of the example. Six squares add to 0.015.

questions.prompt: Four parts each have a tolerance of ±0.05 mm. What is the worst-case stack-up, in ± mm?
hints: In the worst case every tolerance adds.
All four parts stray in the same direction.
Four times 0.05.
questions.onCorrect: A worst-case total assumes that all parts are at an extreme together, so it never underestimates the gap.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the statistical value, from the root of the sum of squares.
That is one part's tolerance. Add all four.

questions.prompt: Hole 25.000 to 25.021 mm, shaft 24.980 to 24.993 mm. What is the maximum clearance, in mm?
hints: The largest gap is from the largest hole and the smallest shaft.
The largest hole is 25.021 mm.
Subtract 24.980.
questions.onCorrect: The clearance varies from 7 to 41 µm, so a g6 fit is a sliding fit with a small, controlled gap.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the minimum clearance. For the maximum use the largest hole and the smallest shaft.
That is the shaft's tolerance. Subtract the shaft's smallest size from the largest hole.

questions.prompt: In the ISO system, a fit written H7/p6 is usually which kind?
hints: Compare the letter's deviation with the hole's zone.
questions.onCorrect: H7/p6 has the shaft zone entirely above the hole zone, so the parts must be pressed together.

misconceptions.feedback: Clearance fits use shaft letters such as d, f or g. The letter p places the shaft above the hole.
Transition fits use letters such as k or n. With p the zones do not overlap.
A p shaft is above the hole, so there is no gap.

choices.label: A free running clearance fit
An interference fit
A transition fit
A loose fit with a large gap

questions.prompt: Four parts each have a tolerance of ±0.05 mm. What is the worst-case total tolerance, in ± mm?
hints: In the worst case the tolerances add.
Four times 0.05.
The answer is below one quarter of a millimetre.
questions.onCorrect: The statistical total for the same parts is only half as big, which is why design practice often uses it with a check.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the statistical value, from the root of the sum of squares.
That is one part's tolerance. Add all four.

questions.prompt: A polished steel test bar has an ultimate tensile strength of 500 MPa. Roughly what stress amplitude could it survive for an unlimited number of cycles?
hints: Think back to where the S-N curve on the screen before flattens out, compared with the strength it started from.

acceptedIdeas: About half of its strength, near 250 MPa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About half of its strength, near 250 MPa

questions.onCorrect: Half of Su is a rule of thumb for polished steel specimens; real parts have a lower limit once finish, size and notches are included.

misconceptions.feedback: A stress near the tensile strength breaks the bar within a few cycles, and the S-N curve falls well below it.
A steel S-N curve flattens at the endurance limit, and below that level a polished bar is expected to last indefinitely.
That is far below the level at which a steel S-N curve flattens, which for a polished bar is roughly half the tensile strength.

choices.label: None, since any repeated stress breaks steel in the end
About half of its strength, near 250 MPa
About 500 MPa, its full strength
About a tenth of its strength, near 50 MPa

questions.prompt: A plate has a hole with a stress concentration factor Kt = 3, and the nominal stress is 40 MPa. What is the peak stress at the hole, in MPa?
hints: The factor multiplies the nominal stress.
Do not add it to the stress.
Multiply 40 by 3.
questions.onCorrect: The peak stress, not the nominal stress, is what starts the crack, and it sits at the edge of the hole.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the factor. Kt is a multiplier.
That divides. The notch raises the stress.

questions.prompt: A shaft has carried its load for a million cycles without trouble. Why can it still fail on the next cycle?
hints: Think of what a repeated load does at a tiny flaw.

acceptedIdeas: Each cycle can grow a tiny crack a little, so damage builds up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each cycle can grow a tiny crack a little, so damage builds up

questions.onCorrect: Fatigue is cumulative: a crack that is invisible after a million cycles can run through the section in the next hundred thousand.

misconceptions.feedback: The load stays the same from cycle to cycle. The part fails because of what each cycle does to it, not because the load changes.
The material does not weaken evenly. A crack grows from a small flaw.

choices.label: The load rises a little with every cycle until it passes yield
Each cycle can grow a tiny crack a little, so damage builds up
The material weakens evenly with age until it is below yield

questions.prompt: A part has Se = 200 MPa and Su = 500 MPa, with alternating stress sa = 80 MPa and mean stress sm = 100 MPa. Using sa ÷ Se + sm ÷ Su = 1 ÷ n, find the safety factor n, to 2 decimal places.
hints: Work out the two terms: sa ÷ Se and sm ÷ Su.
They are 0.4 and 0.2, and their sum is 0.6.
n is the reciprocal of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: The alternating stress uses two thirds of the fatigue budget and the mean stress a third, which leaves a safety factor of 1.67.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum, which is 1 ÷ n. Take its reciprocal.
That adds the stresses before dividing. Add the two ratios.

questions.prompt: A part has Se = 180 MPa and Su = 450 MPa, with sa = 60 MPa and sm = 90 MPa. What is the Goodman safety factor n, to 2 decimal places?
hints: sa ÷ Se is one third, and sm ÷ Su is 0.2.
Add them: 0.5333.
questions.onCorrect: A safety factor below 1 would put the stress state outside the Goodman line, which is the boundary of safe infinite life.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum, which is 1 ÷ n. Take its reciprocal.
That is the ratio of the stresses. Use the Goodman sum of ratios.

questions.prompt: A part sees 10⁵ cycles at a stress whose life is N = 4 × 10⁵, and 2 × 10⁵ cycles at a stress whose life is N = 10⁶. Using Miner's rule, what is the total damage?
hints: Damage from each block is its cycles divided by its life.
The first is 0.25.
The second is 0.2.
questions.onCorrect: Failure is predicted when the total reaches 1, so this part has used 45% of its life.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first block's damage alone. Add the second.
That adds the cycle counts and divides once. Add the two ratios separately.

questions.prompt: Damage of 0.45 has been used up. Under the first stress, where N = 4 × 10⁵ cycles, how many more cycles can the part take before the total damage reaches 1?
hints: The damage left is 1 minus the damage used.
Multiply that by the life N.
questions.onCorrect: Miner's rule treats the life as a budget of 1, so what is left can be spent at any stress in proportion to its life.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole life at this stress. Only the fraction left may be used.
That is the damage used times the life. Use the fraction that remains.

questions.prompt: A part has Se = 250 MPa and Su = 600 MPa, with sa = 75 MPa and sm = 120 MPa. What is the safety factor n, to 2 decimal places?
hints: sa ÷ Se = 0.3 and sm ÷ Su = 0.2.
They sum to 0.5.
n is 1 divided by the sum.
questions.onCorrect: The sum of the two ratios is 0.5, half of the Goodman limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 1 ÷ n. Take the reciprocal.
Add the two ratios, not the stresses.

questions.prompt: 0.25 of a part's life is used at one stress and 0.3 at another. What is the total damage by Miner's rule?
hints: Miner's rule adds damage fractions.
Each fraction is the share of life used at one stress.
Add 0.25 and 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: A total of 0.55 means a little under half of the fatigue life is left.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the fractions. Miner's rule adds them.
Check the sum.

questions.prompt: A hole gives Kt = 2.5 on a nominal stress of 60 MPa. What is the peak stress, in MPa?
hints: The factor multiplies the nominal stress.
Do not add it to the stress.
Multiply 60 by 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: The notch makes the local stress 2.5 times the average, and that peak is where the fatigue crack starts.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the factor. Kt is a multiplier.
That divides. The notch raises the stress.

questions.prompt: Three bars are pinned together at their ends in a triangle, and one of them is bolted down as the frame. What happens when you push on one of the other two bars?
hints: Ask whether any corner of the triangle could move without one of the bars changing its length.
questions.onCorrect: A triangle of rigid bars cannot change its shape, which is why a truss built of triangles is rigid.

misconceptions.feedback: For that bar to swing, the distance between the two free ends of the triangle would have to change, and the third bar, being rigid, fixes that distance.
The two free bars share a pin at the top corner, and that pin can only sit at the one point that is the right distance from both ends of the frame, so neither bar can swing.

choices.label: Both bars swing, each about its pin on the frame
The pushed bar swings and drags the third bar with it
Neither bar can move

questions.prompt: Four links are 30, 40, 60 and 60 mm. Is this loop Grashof?
hints: Name the shortest and the longest link, s and l, and add the other two.
A loop is Grashof when s + l ≤ p + q.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, some link can turn fully
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, some link can turn fully

questions.onCorrect: Equal lengths make no difference to the test, which compares only the two sums.

misconceptions.feedback: Add the shortest and the longest, 30 + 60, and add the other two, 40 + 60. The loop is Grashof when the first sum is no larger than the second.
Equal lengths do not affect the test, which compares only the shortest plus the longest with the other two.
The test uses only the four lengths. The choice of frame decides which link turns, not whether one can.

choices.label: No, no link can turn fully
No, because two of the links have the same length
It cannot be said until the frame is chosen
Yes, some link can turn fully

questions.prompt: With the crank at 180° the 20, 50, 40, 60 mm linkage has a transmission angle of 125.1° between coupler and rocker. How well does it pass force to the rocker in that position?
hints: Judge the angle by how far it is from a straight line, 0° or 180°.

acceptedIdeas: Well, because 125.1° is 54.9° from a straight line, comfortably above the guide of about 40°
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Well, because 125.1° is 54.9° from a straight line, comfortably above the guide of about 40°

questions.onCorrect: Here sin 125.1° = 0.82, slightly more than the 0.78 at the other extreme.

misconceptions.feedback: What matters is the angle's distance from a straight line, and 125.1° is 54.9° from one, so sin 125.1° = 0.82 of the push still turns the rocker.
Jamming comes as the angle approaches 0° or 180°, and at 54.9° from a straight line the rocker still receives 0.82 of the push.
An angle past 90° only means that the coupler leans the other way; the linkage still moves and passes 0.82 of the push.

choices.label: Not at all, because a linkage cannot move once the angle passes a right angle
Well, because 125.1° is 54.9° from a straight line, comfortably above the guide of about 40°
Badly, because 54.9° from a straight line is close to jamming
Badly, because the angle is more than 90°

questions.prompt: A drawing allows a 25 mm shaft to be anywhere between 24.980 mm and 24.993 mm, rather than giving one exact size. Why does it give a range?
hints: Ask what would happen if the drawing demanded exactly 24.987 mm.

acceptedIdeas: Because no machine can cut every part to exactly one size
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because no machine can cut every part to exactly one size

questions.onCorrect: Any shaft inside the range is a good one, however close it sits to either limit.

misconceptions.feedback: The range is set so that any shaft in it fits any hole made to its own range, with no matching of one part to another.
The range describes the size the shaft may have when it is made, and wear in service is a separate matter.

choices.label: To allow for the shaft wearing down in service
So that the machinist can match the shaft to a hole already made
Because no machine can cut every part to exactly one size

questions.prompt: Two bars lie in a plane, and neither is fixed to the frame. They are pinned together at one end by a pin joint. How many freedoms do the two bars have between them?
hints: Count the freedoms the two bars have before they are joined.
Each free bar has three, so the pair has six before the pin takes any away.
Take away what the pin removes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two free bars have 3 + 3 = 6 freedoms, and the pin removes 2, which leaves 4.

questions.onCorrect: The pair can still move as one body, which uses three freedoms, and the second bar can also turn about the pin, which is the fourth.

misconceptions.feedback: Six is the count for two bars that are not yet joined. The pin takes some of those freedoms away.
A pin joint removes two freedoms, not one.
One is what a single bar has when it is pinned to the frame. Here neither bar is held, so the pair can still move.
Three is the count for one free bar. Count both bars before the pin takes any away.

questions.prompt: Links of 20, 55, 60 and 70 mm form a loop with the 55 mm link as the frame and the 20 mm link as the coupler, opposite the frame. What kind of linkage is it?
hints: First test the four lengths with s + l and p + q.
Then see where the shortest link sits relative to the frame.
questions.onCorrect: The sums are 90 and 115, so the loop is Grashof, and the shortest link, opposite the frame, turns fully while both links pinned to the frame only rock.

choices.label: Crank-rocker
Double-crank
Triple-rocker
Double-rocker

misconceptions.feedback: A crank-rocker has the shortest link next to the frame as the crank. Here the shortest link is opposite the frame.
A double-crank has the shortest link as the frame. Here the frame is the 55 mm link.
A triple-rocker has no link that can turn fully. Test the lengths with s + l and p + q before deciding.

questions.prompt: A linkage has transmission angles of 45°, 75°, 110° and 165° at four positions of its crank. At which position does it pass the least of the coupler's push to the rocker?
hints: Judge each angle by how far it is from a straight line, 0° or 180°.
The nearer an angle is to a straight line, the less of the push turns the rocker.
questions.onCorrect: 165° is only 15° from a straight line, so sin 165° = 0.26 and about a quarter of the push turns the rocker, while most of it squeezes the pin.

misconceptions.feedback: 45° is 45° from a straight line, which is above the guide of about 40°. What counts is the distance from a straight line, not the size of the angle.
75° is 15° from a right angle, so most of the push turns the rocker. Compare how far each angle is from 0° or 180°.
110° is 70° from a straight line, which passes more of the push than 45° does. An angle past 90° only means the coupler leans the other way.

questions.prompt: A linkage has a 15 mm crank, 50 mm coupler, 50 mm rocker and 30 mm frame. With the crank at 0° the crank pin is 15 mm from the rocker pin. Find the transmission angle in degrees, to 1 decimal place, from cos μ = (50² + 50² − 15²) ÷ (2 × 50 × 50).
hints: Work out the top of the fraction first.
The top is 4775 and the bottom is 5000.
Take the inverse cosine.
questions.onCorrect: At 17.3° only sin μ, about 30%, of the coupler's force turns the rocker, so a load would nearly jam this position.

misconceptions.feedback: That is cos μ. Find the angle whose cosine it is.
That is 90° less the answer. Take the inverse cosine of the fraction itself.

questions.prompt: With r = 30 mm and l = 120 mm and the crank at 90°, how far is the slider from the crank centre, in millimetres, to 1 decimal place?
hints: At 90° the cos term vanishes.
You need √(l² − r²).
14400 − 900 is the number under the root.
questions.onCorrect: The slider is 3.8 mm short of the rod length here, and the shorter the rod the larger that shortfall.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the tilt of the rod.
That is l − r, the position at the inner end of the stroke.

questions.prompt: A quick-return offset gives α = 45°. What is the ratio of the forward-stroke time to the return-stroke time, to 1 decimal place?
hints: The forward stroke uses 180° + α of crank turn.
The two crank turns are 225° and 135°.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: Of each cycle, 225 of the 360 degrees, 62.5%, go to the forward stroke and 37.5% to the return.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down: the longer stroke goes on top.
Divide 225 by 135, not 225 by 180.

questions.prompt: Because the speed is the same from the first instant of the rise to the last, the follower has to go from rest to full speed in no time at all. What acceleration does that call for at the start?
hints: Acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time it takes.

acceptedIdeas: An infinite acceleration, for an instant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An infinite acceleration, for an instant

questions.onCorrect: A jump in speed in no time needs an infinite acceleration, which in practice is a hammer blow on the follower.

choices.label: None, because the speed is constant
An infinite acceleration, for an instant
A small acceleration, spread over the rise

misconceptions.feedback: The speed is constant during the rise, but it has to reach that value from rest, and that change needs an acceleration at the first instant.

questions.prompt: A cycloidal rise of 36 mm takes 0.4 s. What is the peak speed in mm/s?
hints: The average speed is lift ÷ time.
The average is 90 mm/s.
Cycloidal peak is twice that.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Average = 36 ÷ 0.4 = 90 mm/s, so the peak is 2 × 90 = 180 mm/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average. Double it for the cycloidal peak.
That is the simple harmonic peak, π/2 times 90.

questions.prompt: A small fan motor starts and stops every few minutes and runs only briefly each time. Why would a rolling bearing suit it better than a plain bearing?
hints: Think about what a plain bearing has between shaft and bush once the shaft is turning, and what it has before.

acceptedIdeas: A plain bearing's surfaces touch at every start, before its oil film forms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A plain bearing's surfaces touch at every start, before its oil film forms

questions.onCorrect: The oil film forms only once the shaft drags oil into the gap, so each start is a short spell of metal touching metal, which a rolling bearing largely avoids.

choices.label: A plain bearing's surfaces touch at every start, before its oil film forms
A plain bearing is too noisy when it is run in short bursts
A rolling bearing's contact stresses are lower, so it wears less at start-up

misconceptions.feedback: A plain bearing is quiet when it is running. The trouble with short runs lies in what happens before the shaft is up to speed.
The contact areas in a rolling bearing are tiny, so its contact stresses are very large, and that limits its life. The advantage in short runs lies elsewhere.

questions.prompt: L10 = 216 million revolutions at 1200 rpm. How many hours is that, to the nearest whole hour?
hints: Revolutions per hour = 60 × 1200.
That is 72,000 revolutions an hour.
Divide 216 × 10⁶ by it.
questions.onCorrect: At 1200 rpm a bearing rated for 216 million revolutions runs for 3000 hours, about four months of continuous running.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the life in million revolutions. Convert to hours.

questions.onCorrect: The wire's surface is shorter on the inside of the coil, so the stress there is higher than in a straight bar, and tight coils raise it most.

choices.label: The wire is stretched along its length as well as being twisted
The curved coil raises the stress on the inside of each turn
The Wahl factor adds a safety margin on top of the basic stress

misconceptions.feedback: The wire is not stretched. The load twists it, and the extra stress comes from the shape the wire is bent into.
The factor is not a safety margin. It corrects the calculated stress to the stress the wire actually has.

questions.prompt: Springs of 10 N/mm and 15 N/mm are joined in series. What is the combined rate in N/mm?
hints: Flexibilities add in series.
Invert.
questions.onCorrect: The series rate is lower than either spring's rate, which is why a series chain of springs is soft.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the rates, which is the rule for parallel.
That is the average. In series, flexibilities add.

questions.prompt: A mass of 0.2 kg is on a spring of rate 5000 N/m. What is the natural frequency in Hz, to 1 decimal place?
hints: Divide k by m.
Divide by 2π.
questions.onCorrect: A light mass on a stiff spring gives a high frequency, and a load pulsing near 25 Hz would excite resonance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is ω in rad/s. Divide by 2π.
That is k ÷ m. Take the square root and divide by 2π.

questions.prompt: A bolt has a preload of 24 kN and the joint constant is 0.25. What external load separates the joint, in kN?
hints: Use P = Fi ÷ (1 − C).
Divide the preload by that.
questions.onCorrect: At 32 kN the clamp force is gone, and the bolt alone carries everything.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the preload alone. Divide by 1 − C to find separation.
That multiplies by 0.75. Divide by it.

questions.prompt: A fit that can leave a small gap or a small squeeze, depending on which two parts are paired, is called a ___ fit.
hints: The shaft's size band overlaps the hole's, so this fit sits between the other two kinds.
questions.onCorrect: In a transition fit the two size bands overlap, so one pair may have a small gap and another a small squeeze.

misconceptions.feedback: A clearance fit has a gap at every size. This fit can have a gap or a squeeze.
An interference fit has the shaft larger than the hole at every size. This fit can go either way.

questions.prompt: Hole 40.000 to 40.025 mm, shaft 39.975 to 39.991 mm. What is the maximum clearance, in mm?
hints: The largest gap is from the largest hole and the smallest shaft.
The largest hole is 40.025 mm.
Subtract 39.975.
questions.onCorrect: The clearance varies from 9 to 50 µm, so a g6 fit is a sliding fit with a small, controlled gap.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the minimum clearance. For the maximum use the largest hole and the smallest shaft.
That is the shaft's tolerance. Subtract the shaft's smallest size from the largest hole.

questions.prompt: Five parts each have a tolerance of ±0.06 mm. What is the worst-case total tolerance, in ± mm?
hints: In the worst case the tolerances add.
Five times 0.06.
questions.onCorrect: The statistical total for the same parts is about ±0.13 mm, less than half of this, which is why design practice often uses it with a check.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the statistical value, from the root of the sum of squares.
That is one part's tolerance. Add all five.

questions.prompt: A part sees 10⁵ cycles at a stress whose life is N = 4 × 10⁵. Using Miner's rule, what fraction of its life does this block use?
hints: The fraction used is the cycles divided by the life.
The life is 4 × 10⁵ = 400 000 cycles.
questions.onCorrect: A quarter of the life is used up. Failure is predicted when the fractions from all the blocks add to 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the life divided by the cycles. Miner's fraction is the cycles divided by the life.
That divides by 10⁶. The life at this stress is N = 4 × 10⁵.

flashcards.front: What do we call the number of independent inputs a planar mechanism needs?
flashcards.back: It is the mobility, M = 3(n − 1) − 2×j1 − j2.

flashcards.front: Why does a mobility of 1 not make a mechanism weak or slow?
flashcards.back: It means one input fully decides the motion, which is what a machine needs.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the link in a four-bar that is fixed to the ground?
flashcards.back: The frame is the fixed link, and it is the reference for the motion of the other three.

flashcards.front: State Grashof's test for a four-bar linkage.
flashcards.back: If the shortest plus the longest link is at most the sum of the other two, a link can turn fully.

flashcards.front: What is the stroke of a slider-crank called when it is stretched out and folded, in terms of the crank radius r?
flashcards.back: The ends of travel are l + r and l − r, so the stroke is 2r.

flashcards.front: Why is the slider's speed zero at each end of its stroke?
flashcards.back: The slider reverses direction there, so it stops for an instant at each dead centre.

flashcards.front: What do we call the part of a displacement diagram in which the follower stays still while the cam turns?
flashcards.back: A dwell is a period in which the follower does not move, and the cam outline there is a circular arc.

flashcards.front: Why is constant-velocity motion not the gentlest law for a cam?
flashcards.back: Its speed jumps from rest to full at the ends of the rise, which needs infinite acceleration and hammers the follower.

flashcards.front: What name is given to the pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth?
flashcards.back: The module m = d ÷ z, in millimetres, sets the size of the teeth.

flashcards.front: A gear of module 2 mm has 30 teeth. What is its outside diameter in mm?
flashcards.back: The outside diameter is m(z + 2) = 2 × 32 = 64 mm.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The outside diameter is m(z + 2) = 2 × 32 = 64 mm.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the part of a planetary set that carries the planet gears?
flashcards.back: The carrier holds the planets' axes, and it is usually where the output is taken.

flashcards.front: Why is a worm drive not always self-locking?
flashcards.back: It locks only when the lead angle is below the friction angle, and a steeper thread has a larger lead angle.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the component of tooth force that acts along the line between the two gear centres?
flashcards.back: The radial force pushes the gears apart and loads the bearings; it is Ft tan φ.

flashcards.front: A solid shaft's diameter is tripled at the same torque. By what factor does the maximum shear stress fall?
flashcards.back: Stress goes as 1 ÷ d³, so tripling d divides it by 3³ = 27.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Stress goes as 1 ÷ d³, so tripling d divides it by 3³ = 27.

flashcards.front: A ball bearing has C = 10 kN and P = 2 kN. What is L10 in million revolutions?
flashcards.back: L10 = (C ÷ P)³ = 5³ = 125 million revolutions.

flashcards.front: Why does L10 not tell you how long each bearing will last?
flashcards.back: It is the life that 90% of identical bearings reach, so about 10% fail sooner and the median bearing lasts about five times longer.

flashcards.front: What name is given to the ratio of coil diameter to wire diameter, D ÷ d?
flashcards.back: The spring index C = D ÷ d, which sets the size of the Wahl factor.

flashcards.front: Why do springs in series add their flexibilities and not their stiffnesses?
flashcards.back: The same force passes through each, so the deflections add, and deflection per unit force is flexibility.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the ratio kb ÷ (kb + km) of bolt stiffness to total joint stiffness?
flashcards.back: The joint constant C is the share of an external load that the bolt carries.

flashcards.front: Why does the bolt carry only a small share of an external load?
flashcards.back: The clamped parts are much stiffer, so they give up their squeeze while the bolt stretches only slightly.

flashcards.front: In ISO limits, which capital letter marks a hole whose lower deviation is zero?
flashcards.back: The letter H places the hole's tolerance band just above nominal size.

flashcards.front: Why is a tolerance not an error?
flashcards.back: It is a permission to vary: any size inside the band is acceptable, and a tighter band costs more.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the stress level below which a steel part is expected never to fail by fatigue?
flashcards.back: The endurance limit Se is the flat part of the S-N curve for steels.

flashcards.front: Why is a stress concentration factor multiplied and not added?
flashcards.back: It raises the stress in proportion at the notch, so the peak is Kt times the nominal stress.
